en: Now begins the first chapter:
O Teacher of the World, tell me how Viṣṇu, the Lord of all worlds and the Sovereign who performs the eightfold acts beginning with creation, brought forth the entire universe.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"Nārāyaṇa is of infinite power, perfect bliss, imperishable, and the self-sovereign ruler;
he possesses an infinite body consisting of knowledge and bliss—such is the Vedic revelation. (PS 1.1.2)
Even Ramā, Brahmā, and the others do not know at all the true nature of that independent, great-souled Hari in its entirety.
Nevertheless, I shall explain it to you so that you may know it according to reality:
for Him whose desires are fulfilled, there is no purpose in creation and the like.
Such is its intrinsic nature that the Unborn performs that for that purpose; He alone is the Blessed Lord, the Self, the regulator of the moving and the unmoving.
The Supreme Person, the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, in the form of Nṛsiṃha, devoured all the material egg-shells.
Then, having placed within his own belly all sentient beings— both those liberated in previous kalpas and those still bound— the Blessed One, self-luminous, slept happily.
The measurement of the existence of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is endowed with ten coverings,
is equal to the extent of space occupied by the venerable one in the form of Rudra.
The ground was formerly as beautiful as a banyan leaf;
it was limited by that much [space] and was of the nature of darkness.
At that time, there was nothing else outside except for Ramā;
all living beings then resided within the womb of the child named Śūnya.
Those [souls] situated in the upper part of the belly become liberated in the Great Abode (mahālaya);
those in the middle of the belly are fit for liberation; but those on the sides are eternally bound.
Those below, in the region of the gods, experience suffering at the level of their hips;
those above them dwell in fashioned bliss. Only the liberated ones enjoy that [bliss], and no others.
Mādhava will grant to them, through dissolution alone, those things they are destined to obtain—
having abandoned the bliss that is already attained, for they are those who enjoy only the bliss prepared [for them].

O Lotus-born One, it is said that Hari abandons his pastimes in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms to dwell within a womb, and that at the time of dissolution, all liberated souls undergo destruction. PS_1,1.14.

The multitudes of individual souls (jīvas) are worthy of experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth; they consist of the nature of will and knowledge, and are devoted to aversion, merit, demerit, and effort. (PS 1.15)
Indeed, all individual souls wander in the process of creation, bound by their subtle bodies;
having entered a state of equilibrium, they are endowed with these subtle forms.
When the primordial power enters the womb of Vasantīśa,
then all such beings fall into a profound sleep.
The wise say that there is "dissolution" (laya), yet in its own nature, dissolution does not exist; for the powers of knowledge and action abide within the very nature of all living beings.
The power of the Śruti to bestow knowledge through the activity of the mind is held to be such that,
in the state of dissolution where the individual soul and so forth are absent, that power becomes blunted.
The dissolution of the Vedas, which are the abodes of the intellect of the Lord of Pervasion,
as well as of the cosmic egg, the insentient, and the individual souls, is into that which is designated as space and the unmanifest.
At the time of creation, this is the substratum; at dissolution, it becomes inert.
This cessation of the unmanifested space is called "dissolution" (laya). (PS 1.21)
In the process of creation, there exists a power that leads all embodied beings, according to their respective karmas, to various wombs; however, this is not the case during dissolution.
The power that bestows pleasure and pain for all performed actions is not blunted by Viṣṇu’s command during creation or dissolution.
For such a dissolution of that [word] is not considered a dissolution of its own nature;
rather, it is maintained that the power to manifest all languages resides in the phonemes. (PS 1.1.24)
It does not exist during creation, for their destruction at the time of dissolution is of such a nature;
the dissolution of those situated in darkness is recorded as the experiencing of previously ordained suffering.
[The knowledge] of the linga consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as of inert primordial nature itself,
of the subtle elements in their state of grossness, and of the three qualities (triguṇa) in their entirety.

For the power of creation exists in the act of creating, not in dissolution; therefore, dissolution occurs when one abandons the creation of the world and so forth, remaining forever devoted to the Lord of Śrī.
For service that is too close is proclaimed to be the ruin of prosperity,
whether it be toward that which is impermanent and insentient, or even toward that which is within or outside the cosmic egg.
The burning and destruction resulting from the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa are said to occur gradually;
yet all castes, pervading both space and time, are eternal.
Prakṛti is insentient, eternal, and indeed atomic in its insentient form;
yet it is always pervaded by the conscious nature of Śrī Hari throughout space and time.
Inferior in terms of infinite qualities compared to the Lord who possesses infinite qualities,
they all, having resorted to dissolution, dwell there with their powers exhausted.
In the Lord Hari, who is infinite and possesses complete power throughout space and time, there eternally exist infinite and endless forms, even as small as a single atom.
Hari, the Supreme, is non-different from that [consciousness] and possesses infinite subtle and gross forms;
he has as his essential nature the vast, subtle, and gross forms of all individual souls.
Hari, the teacher of the world, who consists of all inert matter and possesses infinite and endless forms,
is devoid of qualities and remains non-different even from those infinite and endless beings.
The Self has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere;
possessing all sense organs everywhere, it stands pervading everything.
Possessing infinite forms with extraordinary senses, most wonderful,
unattached and all-knowing, devoid of qualities yet filled with qualities.
He exists both outside and inside all beings, as the unmoving and the moving;
he is the unmanifest and the manifest form, the virtuous one who is the object of perception for the witness of existence.
Though one, he appears as many; he is eternal, true, and great bliss;
he is accessible through infinite Vedas and is the Lord who performs the eightfold acts beginning with creation.
The body of consciousness (cittanu), which is independent, vast, and infinite,
resides within a single part of the center of its own infinite and infinite body consisting of pure consciousness alone.
Having entered yogic sleep, Hari, the Lord who is himself sleepless,
burns away the accumulation of the covering of the cosmic egg during the dissolution.
Having unified the material cause (upādāna) by its very nature, the Man-Lion [manifests];
from the Man-Lion [form] comes Saṅkarṣaṇa, with Aniruddha and the others situated in his mouth.
Having burned away the accumulation of all subtle bodies, the unborn Lord of All unifies their constituent materials with the subtle bodies (liṅgas).
Then Śrī, in the form of his wife, became the ground for the spreading of that [seat];
Durgā, in the form of a covering, belonged to Hari of immeasurable splendor.
Enjoying only his own excellent qualities, Viṣṇu remained as if in deep sleep though he was not asleep; his belly was empty of all that is enjoyed, and he is the vast light of infinite infinities.
Self-luminous, yet fallen into the sleep of yoga-nidrā upon the leaf of the banyan tree, at the time of creation all living beings are overwhelmed by various sufferings. (PS 1.1.45)
They revolve for the cessation of the various labors of all living beings;
at the time of dissolution, they cause those bound by their subtle bodies who reside within their own physical forms to attain sleep.

[He creates] many objects of creation who are agitated by ignorance regarding the state of karma and its lack of beginning, who possess diverse characteristics, who exist in varying degrees [of merit], and who are of threefold nature.
The Asuras, who experience only suffering, are always possessed of very little sleep, great sleep, and deep sleep, whereas the liberated ones enjoy the bliss of pure consciousness alone.
Having placed those who dwell in darkness and are eternally bound within his belly, Keśava,
the Lord whose feet are the refuge, seems to practice sleep upon a leaf of the banyan tree.

Having himself created the objects to be emanated within them, the omnipresent Lord desired, at the end of his dissolution, to bestow upon them happiness, mixed states, and likewise suffering, according to their respective merits.
The eighth part of *laya* is declared to be the final *laya*;
in that *laya*, the Supreme Goddess, free from sleep, embraces Hari.
Or when [the universe] is asleep, the Śrīdevī, having resorted to the ocean of eternal bliss, remains dependent upon her own sovereignty during the eighth part of the dissolution.
And having been awakened by the command of Viṣṇu, she began to praise him;
[a praise] which was infinite in terms of place and time, yet devoid of the infinity of qualities.
The beloved of Viṣṇu is superior to Brahmā and Vāyu by ten millionfold; she is the presiding deity over dissolution, creation, and all eternal entities. (PS 1.1.54)
By the command of Viṣṇu, she who possesses infinite forms performs the eightfold acts beginning with creation;
like a shadow, she rests upon Viṣṇu, assuming subtle, gross, and vast forms.
Directly perceiving the qualities of Viṣṇu, which are proclaimed even beyond the end in his infinite Vedas, she is the personification of all the Vedas.
Possessing beauty beyond description, she is the one who takes pride in all living beings;
she is the radiant Śrī, white and worthy of liberation, who takes pride in those who are pure and fit for release.
Among all those bound by attachment, the earth-element presides with the conceit of being red;
among those unworthy beings who are blue, Durgā presides with the conceit of being blue.

Prakṛti is the initiator of equilibrium, disequilibrium, and so forth within Prakṛti itself; she is uninterrupted in her devotion to the Blessed One, and though she takes a material form among insentient things, she remains [transcendent]. (PS 1.1.59)
In women, she is of the nature of pure consciousness and is the initiator of feminine gestures and the like;
she possesses a superior male form, yet is entirely devoid of the state of being male.
Devoid of a body composed of the unmanifest and its effects,
Śrī herself— knowing the state of Viṣṇu and conversant with the Vedas— praised the Knower of the Vedas.
Those Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharvaṇa—are under the control of Śrī Hari;
all four are distinct in their origins, infinite, and free from defects.
The sequence of phonemes, including the accents such as the udātta and so forth, their meanings, and their conjunctions,
is established through the collection of qualities appropriate for the words preceded by the visarga, bindu, and pūrva-uru.
Beginning from infinite time, they are devoid of even slight error; possessing parts, they pervade all locations, and are eternally pure and insentient.

Those [scriptures] devoted to proclaiming the qualities of Viṣṇu and free from defects of sound possess the quality of making known what is already known; in them, there is no speaking of contrary meanings. (PS 1.1.65)
In those [sounds], defects of speech such as indistinctness and so forth do not exist at all;
they are of the nature of resonance (dhvani), existing at the time of creation, situated in speech, and under the control of the Goddess of Speech.
In the creation, they are brought under the control of Lakṣmī by the presiding deities such as Brahmā;
protected during dissolution, they indeed become uniform again at the time of creation.
Countless upon countless are those who are practitioners of Viṣṇu’s knowledge;
infinite in every land, they reside within the throat of that wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Chanted by the throat, they manifest the knowledge of the respective essential natures of living beings according to their individual fitness and by the will of Śrī Hari. (PS 1.1.69)
Skilled in the production of functional cognitions, they do not cause the understanding of meanings that are unfit [for verbal expression].
Having the nature of sound, they are perceived solely by the ear together with the mind and the witness-consciousness.
Durgā, who possesses infinite forms, consists of the nature of all sounds; she is the reflection of the image of Hari, whose essence is all sound, appearing in the form of words within the Vedas.

Knowing that the Supreme Person was to be awakened, he, whose self is infinite and whose power is infinite, praised the Supreme Person with a multitude of Vedic hymns beginning with the syllable *oṃ*.
Manifesting the eternal [Vedas], he taught the Durgā [mantra] for their creation during the eighth part of the dissolution of the Lord of the World, the creator of the Vedas.

The syllable Oṃ (A) first became manifest as consisting of the Blessed One; from it arose the vowels (Ā, I, etc.), the nasal sounds (Anusvāra), the bindus, the resonant sounds (Ghoṣa), the Silent (Śānta), and the Transcendentally Silent (Atiśānta).

O sons, you are eternally composed of consciousness; you are the very nature of Viśva and the others, you are denoted by that [Oṃ], you are contained within that, and you are the Supreme Person denoted by the syllable Oṃ.
These [names] are the designators of Hari’s forms— the Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya— which are the inner selves consisting of the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
The syllable Om, which is denoted by the words *tāra* and *praṇava*,
is said to have arisen from the syllables containing the seed-essence (*tara*) within the eight-syllabled mantra known as Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, Abhivyakta, Viśva, and so forth— all these, beginning with Vyakta-Viśva,
are proclaimed to be the deities denoted by the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
The mantra known as the Vyāhṛtis arose from the first four syllables containing the seed *tāra*;
those beginning with Aniruddha and Viśva were uttered by him.
The fifty phonemes are said to be manifested by the syllables containing the *tāra* (the sacred syllable *oṃ*) as their core;
likewise, the eight [phonemes] beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa* have been illustrated.
The eight vowels arising from the letter *a* are recognized as sixteen;
the five letters of the *ka*-group are proclaimed to arise from the letter *u*.
The five letters of the *ca*-group are proclaimed to arise from the letter *ma*;
the five letters of the *ṭa*-group, however, are considered to arise from the *nāda*.
The five vowels of the *tavarga* are said to be manifested by the *bindu*;
indeed, the five vowels of the *pavarga* arise from the voiced sounds (*ghoṣa*).
The four letters of the *ya*-group will attain manifestation through tranquility;
from extreme tranquility, the five letters of the *śa*-group have arisen.
Manifested through the application of effort, it is called the syllable that is to be shaken (*kṣoṇya*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*).
It consists of fifty phonemes, along with the eight deities of the syllable *Tāra*.
The deities beginning with Aja are considered to be manifested by the [syllables] beginning with Viśva in sequence:
Aja, Ānanda, Indra, Īśa, Ugra, Ūrja, and Ṛtambhara. (PS 1.86)
Ṛghaḥ, ḷśau, lṝji, reka, ātmai, ra, ojobhṛt, aurasaḥ, antaḥ, ūrdhagarbhaḥ, kapilaḥ, khapatiḥ, garuḍāsanaḥ.
Gharma, Uṅgasāra, Cārvaṅga, Chandogamya, Janārdana, Jhaḍitārin, Amaṣṭaṅkin, Ṭhalaka, Ḍaraka, and Ḍharī. PS_1.1.88.
The Self, the Savior, the One with the Raised Staff, the Archer, the Subduer, the Supreme, the Fruitful,
Bali, Bhaga, Manu, the Sacrifice, Rāma, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Excellent One.
Śāntasaṃvit, Ṣaḍguṇa, Sārātman, Haṃsa, and Lāluka—
these are proclaimed to be denotable by all the letters beginning with 'a'.
Nṛsiṃha, who is to be praised, is the controller of all living beings;
he is declared to be the Mātṛkā-mantra consisting of fifty-one syllables.
The eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa and the twelve-syllable mantra of Vāsudeva, when combined with the four *vyāhṛtis* in sequence, became the Great Self (*mahadātmaka*).
The twelve deities corresponding to the syllables of those mantras begin with Keśava;
these mantras were spoken three times by Viṣṇu himself, and they originated from Nārāyaṇa.
The Gāyatrī has Brahmā as its seer (ṛṣi); from the twelve syllables doubled [there are twenty-four], and Keśava and the others are the twenty-four deities of the letters of the Gāyatrī.
From the Gāyatrī comes the Puruṣa-sūkta; from the Sūkta come the Vaiṣṇava mantras.
That Puruṣa who is expounded by the Puruṣa-sūkta is declared to be Hari. (PS 1.1.95)
Viṣṇu, invoked by the Viṣṇu-mantra, is proclaimed as the Self of all;
[this consists of] the Praṇava, the eight Vyāhṛtis, the Mātṛkās, and the twelve-syllable [mantra].
The Gāyatrī with Brahmā as its seer, and likewise the Puṃsūkta which belongs to Viṣṇu—
these eight great Vedic mantras bestow all accomplishments.
The Śruti declares that from the Puruṣasūkta, the manifestation of all the Vedas arose;
thus Hari, whose forms are infinite, was proclaimed by the infinite Vedas through Durgā, who possesses infinite forms.
Requested by her, the Lord of All fashioned the creation of his own self.
Thus ends the first chapter of the first section in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā* within the *Śrī Paratattvanirṇaya*.
Śrī Haṃsa said:
Having been thus praised, Keśava then arose.
Then Hari assumed a body named Śūnya, also known as Paruṣa.
The Puruṣa stands like the unmanifest seed of all forms;
he is called the infinite self, whose body is all-pervading and whose belly is the universe.
From Puruṣa, the four beginning with Vāsudeva then came into being:
namely, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Vāsudeva and the others are white, red, yellow, and blue respectively; Hari assumes these bodies of his own will for liberation, enjoyment, concealment, and creation.
The goddess Ramā, whose name is Śūnyā, having become Śrī, took refuge in the Puruṣa; she herself, becoming Māyā and Jayā, is likewise called Kṛti and Śānti.
She was always the non-departing consort of Vāsudeva and others;
Vāsudeva is the four-faced one, the very form of the orb of Brahmā.
Saṅkarṣaṇa has a thousand mouths and the form of the king of serpents;
Pradyumna has the nature of the discus of Māra and possesses an exceedingly beautiful body.
The self of the image belongs to Aniruddha, the son of Kāma;
Hari possesses five forms beginning with the "once-flashing" (sakṛdgholka), as well as the eight bodies beginning with Viśva.
He became the tenfold form beginning with the Fish, whose nature consists of the Vimala and other incarnations;
he became the twelvefold self beginning with Śakti, possessing sixteen forms beginning with Dvārakā.
The one who is higher than the highest was manifested in twenty-three forms beginning with Ānanda;
Hari became possessed of twenty-four forms beginning with Keśava.
Then the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) became manifest in fifty forms beginning with the Unborn (Aja); he then assumed sixty forms known as Time (Kāla), acting as the regulator of the year.
He consists of hundreds beginning with Nārāyaṇa and thousands beginning with Viśva; He exists as infinite forms such as Parādi, yet is devoid of any internal differentiation within Himself.
By her command alone, that goddess Ramā also assumed many forms;
and by her, who possessed infinite forms, the Lord of Ramā likewise became one of infinite forms.
Out of affection for that goddess, the ocean of compassion,
that bull among men, having spent even an eighth part of the time of the dissolution, [remained] for her sake.
At the beginning of the time of creation, he began to create the Unborn One (Aja) and the others.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first section of the *Prakāśasaṃhitā* within the *Śrī Paratattvanirṇaya*.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"Seized by the planets through the aperture of the web [of the heart], the splendor of the sun's rays [descends] upon the earth."
When they stand nearby her, positioned like a crossbar.
When he causes the hair [of the devotee] to stand on end, that atom among mortals—
the supreme among mortals— abides within the Mahar-loka and other realms through the ripening of devotion.
The time that is perceived by one with subtle vision is the atom (paramāṇu);
a hundredth part of that belongs to the gods, and a hundredth part of that belongs to the Son of the Lotus (the Buddha).
That which is an atom (paramāṇu) of time for mortals dwelling on earth is a hundredth part of an atom for one dwelling in the world of the gods.
A ten-millionth part of that [portion] belongs to Ramā, and an infinite-thousandth part of that belongs to Hari;
this is declared to be an atom (paramāṇu), which cannot be perceived by others.
Time consisting of two atoms is called a dyad;
that consisting of three atoms is proclaimed to be a triad. (PS 1.3.6)
A *truṭi* consists of three *tryaṇukas*; a *vedha* consists of three of those;
a *lava* consists of three *vedhas*, and a *nimeṣa* consists of three *lavas*. (PS 1.3.7)
A *kṣaṇa* is said to consist of three *nimeṣas*; five *kṣaṇas* are called a *kāṣṭhā*.
Fifteen *kāṣṭhās* are proclaimed to be a *laghukāla*.
Fifteen laghus are proclaimed to be one vināḍikā;
sixty vināḍikās shall constitute one nāḍikā.
By thirty muhūrtas of those two, a day and night (ahorātra) is said to consist of seven ghaṭikās less one-eighth [of a ghaṭikā] for each.
The time for a watch (yāma) is taught as being seven and a quarter, or indeed seven and a half, or even eight units, according to the division of time.
As many watches as constitute a day, so many are considered to constitute a night;
thirty such days and nights, consisting of two fortnights, make a month. (PS 1.3.12)
By those two [movements], the three seasons and the southern course (ayana) are proclaimed;
when the sun moves through the signs beginning with Cancer and ending with Sagittarius.
The southern course is declared to be known as the night of the gods,
as long as the sun remains from Capricorn up to the end of Gemini.
The period until that [winter solstice] is designated as the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) by the wise; a year is traditionally held to consist of two such courses, each comprising six months.
A year consists of three hundred and sixty days and nights;
it comprises seventeen lakhs and twenty-eight thousand years.
Therefore, the Kṛta Yuga is established [as such], while Tretā is said to be one-quarter less;
it is measured at twelve hundred thousand and ninety-six thousand [years]. (PS 1.3.17)
Then the Tretā Yuga is said to be one-quarter less than that; the Dvāpara is recorded as being sixty-four thousand years, and [the Kṛta] is remembered as measuring eight hundred thousand.
The Kali age is remembered as being half the duration of the Dvāpara age, which is one-quarter [of the full cycle].
Thus, from the sixteen-thousand-year Dvāpara, the Kali age consists of four hundred thousand years.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—these are the four yugas;
the time consisting of these four yugas is called a Mahāyuga.
A period of time calculated by those who perceive time as consisting of twenty thousand, one hundred thousand, and forty-three thousand years is called a Mahāyuga.
Thirty-six hundred years of the gods is said to be one divine year; four thousand such years constitute the age known as Kṛta.
The Tretā age lasts for three thousand years; the Dvāpara is measured at two thousand years; and the Kali is less than that, measuring one thousand years.
At the beginning and at the end of the Kṛta age, there are four hundred years each;
at the beginning and at the end of the junction (saṃdhi) with the Tretā age, there are three hundred years each.
The transition (sandhi) at the end of each pair of ages, such as Dvāpara and so forth, lasts for two hundred years separately;
likewise, the period of transition at the beginning and end of the Kali age is measured at one hundred years.
Thus, by divine measurement, twelve thousand years are reckoned as a period of time known as a Mahāyuga by those who know time.
In eighteen and a half lakhs of years, seventy-one yugas are combined;
this is declared to be the period of the conjunction (manusandhi) and the time of enjoyment.
The dissolution following the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara] lasts for twelve hundred years;
likewise, there is a dissolution at the end of each of the six [manvantaras] beginning with the Svārociṣa.
The period of dissolution is said to consist of fifteen hundred years;
the period of dissolution is also declared to consist of fourteen hundred years. (PS 1.3.29)
In all other Manvantaras, however, this rule always applies;
a thousand cycles of four Yugas is called a single day of Brahmā.
His night is of the same duration, and his day is likewise;
three hundred and sixty such periods are proclaimed as a year for the Unborn One.
A period of one hundred such years is considered the lifespan of the Unborn (Ajā).
From Vāsudeva, at the first moment of his own hundredth year, [the next principle] of subtle form arises.
He who attained a lifespan of one hundred years [did so] from a previous state that was six years and three months older than those other forms.
The subtle creation of the fourfold body consists of the subtle and partial components of those things to be created;
prior to the subtle [creation] of what has been produced, the gross body then came into being.
From Nārāyaṇa, from the Unborn, and from Rudra, creation proceeds sequentially according to time;
as far as there is creation from the subtle, so far is there the gross creation.
Above the egg are the coverings and the gross bodies composed of them;
fifty years of the first Brahmā have passed since that time.
When the day had passed, the creation of the cosmic egg occurred during that night,
while Viṣṇu was sleeping within it in the midst of the waters.
The lotus-born Brahmā arose together with thirty-seven [deities] from within the mundane, ordinary lotus-bud that had not yet emerged from the world. (PS 1.3.38)
At the end of the day and at the end of the night, there is the destruction of the cosmic egg of the Lord of the World;
by means of the reverse order of the previous measurements, there occurs the destruction of the gross and the subtle.
Thus, when the lifespan of those with a hundred-year life has been completed— consisting of two parārdhas—
the Unborn One himself effects the unification of their individual natures.
For as long as it takes for his own creation to reach a state of unification,
he delights even when unified, likewise through the unified Māyā.
After that period, the Unborn causes [the world] to sleep as if in slumber for twice six and a half Brahma-years; this is what I have heard from the learned regarding the end of the night.
Furthermore, in the case of a portion [of the lifespan], the Lord effects the creation of the self and so forth as before;
for that person, no specific measure of life span is prescribed.
Even in such a time, which consists of immeasurable, infinite, and supreme [cycles], Hari, the Lord, will perform the creation and other acts.
The boundary of this independent one cannot be transgressed by those who are not independent;
for everything, both moving and unmoving, is under the control of Him whose power is complete.
Those [states] such as death, birth, and old age belonging to that [self], which have existed for infinite time,
are preceded by exhaustion, suffering, misfortune, anxiety, and torment.
Ignorance, envy, malice, and affliction; desire, anger, fear, and the like; as well as emaciation, disease, misfortune, the taint of merit, and so forth. (PS 1.3.47)
Hope, fear, growth, hunger, thirst, trembling, and the like—
such defects did not exist [in him], nor will they ever exist hereafter in the Lord of All.

And as for the heaps of faults that are imagined by various groups of wicked people against the Merciful One, who is filled with an infinity of virtues opposed to each of those [faults]: [they are nothing]. (PS 1.3.49)
It is certain that even a trace of a scent of those defects does not belong to Viṣṇu;
[this applies to] time, which begins with the atom (paramāṇu) and ends with the period of two parārdhas.
In all those times, the unborn Lord, the husband of Ramā, remains and protects by manifesting His respective powers under each of those names.
This flow of time is eternal, whereas moments and the like are impermanent;
for when existing moments have passed away, others indeed proceed in succession.
This [self], whose nature is indestructible, is the protector of its own stream;
a period of time measured at one hundred years is known as a day of Brahmā.
The time known as a *nimeṣa* (the blink of an eye) is indeed a day for the Supreme Lord;
this is a figurative expression used for the sake of purifying the intellects of ignorant people.
Therefore, the highly wise say that the Lord is infinite in terms of time;
yet the omnipresent one, generating Brahmā, has him as the limit of another period of time.
The Lord of all accepts that time;
even though He is devoid of night, measure, and so forth, the Lord remains for that duration of time.
In this way, acting as night, the Unborn Lord causes Brahmā and the others to sleep;
then, during the final portion of the night, he initiates the creation of himself and the rest.
A person performs [actions], and for that [person] the measure of lifespan is ordained;
thus [the Self] is of the nature of being manifold, immeasurable, infinite, and infinitely supreme.

Time, which is devoid of form and other qualities, is like the essential nature and the senses of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self and the agent of creation and so forth, and it does not transcend [the nature of] time.
For when each preceding period has perished, others indeed come into being from the stream of atoms that are to arrive in the subsequent [period].
The time consisting of ghaṭikās and so forth is to be understood as being equal [to the duration of the breaths];
for ghaṭikās, days, months, and so on do not occur simultaneously.
For Viṣṇu, who is devoid of a measure of lifespan and consists of infinite-infinite supreme selves, knowledge of time is the means for measuring His infinite duration of time.
[He is the cause] of the Vedas, of the syllables, of the teaching, of the unmanifest, of Ramā, of all living beings, and of the liberated ones who possess the subtle body.
Of all the bodies possessing marks, as well as of inert Prakṛti—
of these which are not independent but are subject to the power of the Independent One.
In the measurement of the eternity and infinity of time, the knowledge of time is the necessary means;
[it is] impermanent [and infinite].
And of those who are insentient, as well as of those possessing subtle and gross bodies.
Knowledge of time is the means for determining the lifespan of bodies;
thus, knowing the course of time, one will cross over the fear of time.
At another time, however, the unborn Teacher of the World creates, sustains, and destroys a single world-mandala endowed with its ten enclosures. (PS 1.3.67)
Keśava does not desire to create at any one time a multitude of cosmic eggs,
nor Brahmā, Garuḍa, Śeṣa, Indra, Prāṇa, Ravi, or the gods.
At the time of dissolution, the unborn Hari releases each individual [soul] one by one;
nevertheless, he remains the controller of infinite cosmic eggs (ajāṇḍas), assuming the form of those very eggs.
Hari possesses such great forms; indeed, the Śruti declares that infinite, endless beings dwell upon the infinite pores of Hari's body.
Because of the connection with infinity upon infinity of such infinite forms,
they are joined infinitely below, above, and in the eight directions.
Hari, whose body is full, fills the vast expanse with infinite forms; his form consists of qualities such as supreme non-difference, consciousness, bliss, and power.
He is without distinction, all-pervading, and takes the form of the subtle, the gross, and so forth;
he possesses equal power and auspicious, excellent qualities such as equal knowledge and strength.
And Hari,
who sustains all things conscious and unconscious, delights with Rāmā, who is of infinite forms, who is dependent upon him, and who is the truth of the entire universe.

[The Self] is always distinct from Śrī, who is different [from it]; distinct from the qualities (guṇas) such as liberation, non-liberation, and impurity; distinct from the eternal, insentient, and real [objects]; and always distinct from the individual souls (jīvas) and the Lord (īśvara).
Viṣṇu is distinct from the universe in terms of place and qualities, yet as the all-pervading Lord, Hari—
possessing infinite and endless forms— is non-different while appearing as if he were different.
Even though full, the unborn one, whose nature is both insentient and sentient, creates, sustains, and destroys.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first section of the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*, within the *Śrī Paratattvavarṇana*.
Śrī Haṃsa said:
"The subtle seed of the entire universe, which is measured and protected by Viṣṇu..."
That which the wise call the Pradhāna, the Unmanifest (avyakta). // PS 1.4.1 //
It is called Mahāmāyā, Avidyā, Prakṛti, and Mohinī;
it is the unmanifest consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), possessing three forms, and endowed with three powers (śaktis).
They also know that seed to consist of ignorance, desire, action, and so forth;
it is preserved during dissolution and, at the time of creation, He who possesses infinite forms manifests it.
It is called the knot of beginningless karma, as well as the binder of bondage; it is unborn, not subject to anything else, and joined with the sixteen *kalās*. (PS 1.4.4)
It is said to consist of intense suffering, leading to various states of rebirth,
having a form like a coconut, and being composed of three dimensions.
The divine [ether] at the aperture of the crown is always radiant like a jewel;
it is covered by Viṣṇu and Ramā, possessing an internal space within its opening.
Rama and Māninī are eternally delighted in his creation and dissolution;
likewise, Brahmā and Vāyu, together with their wives, take pride in the act of creation alone.
It is endowed with three constituent parts known as *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*.
The *sattva* portion is white in color, while the *rajas* portion is red in color. (PS 1.4.8)
The dark portion consists of the quality of darkness (tamas) and thus comprises three parts;
the faculties of knowledge and action are established within the portion of passion (rajas). PS 1.4.9.
The five kalās known as the subtle elements (tanmātras) belong to the portion of *tamas*;
the kalā of the mind belongs to the portion of *sattva* and is the primary source of all.

The fourfold [mind] consists of the intellect (manas), the cognitive faculty (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the heart (citta); as well as desire, anger, great greed, pride, envy, delusion, and the like. (PS 1.4.11)
Hatred, egoism, the sense of "mine," envy, malice, fear, and so forth are defects of the mind; that which is free from these is the means for the knowledge of the mind.
The mind is considered to be fourfold and eternally composed of the nature of the insentient (jaḍa-prakṛti).
Even that which is produced from it is impermanent; among these, the *citta* is not possessed of defects.
The mind will generate desire for various objects such as gold and the like; the intellect will constantly form intentions regarding prohibited enjoyments. (PS 1.4.14)
Egoism is the destroyer of the goals of man; together with the most excellent [of men], it incites rivalry and even, in every respect, hatred toward Viṣṇu and the gods.
The mind always makes a person devoted to virtuous means;
however, virtuous means joined with egoism indeed become evil.
Devoid of ego-consciousness, that mind is the instrument of cognition,
just as it assumes a human body when fashioned within the land of Bhārata.
Having attained residence in the teacher’s family through many virtuous births, and having performed the wholesome deeds appropriate for oneself through service to a true guru; PS 1.4.18.

Through hearing the great scriptures and other means taught by those who are serene, that [knowledge] which bestows the knowledge of the mental modes (vṛtti) arises; and devotion to the mental modes and so forth are the means for its accomplishment. (PS 1.4.19)
From those two, devotion to knowledge of one's own true nature will become manifest;
the mind is eternally of that true nature, and from that arises the intellect of that true nature.
That devotion becomes manifest as eternal and likewise as having its own essential nature;
that very same [devotion] abides eternally among the liberated ones in the form of bliss.
They say that all the physical seats of the sense organs are perceptible,
whereas the sense organs themselves are beyond the senses and consist of knowledge and action.
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, and so forth are powers of cognition;
speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are all powers of action. (PS 1.4.23)
The auditory organ perceives sound, and sound is declared to be of two kinds:
that consisting of resonance (dhvani) and that consisting of phonemes (varṇa); of these, the former is the first. (PS 1.4.24)
Arising from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) and being the cause for the production of space, sound whose essence is resonance is proclaimed as the first [element]. (PS 1.4.25)

The subtle elements, consisting of the organs of knowledge, the organs of action, and the mind, are indeed beginningless and eternal; yet they are proclaimed to be non-eternal when created at the time of cosmic manifestation.
That sound which consists of phonemes (varṇa) is eternal, omnipresent, and all-pervading;
in the view of all [schools], it is indeed a substance (dravya), not a quality (guṇa) for anyone. (PS 1.4.27)
The Vedas, whether by their words, syllables, sounds, or accents,
are all beginningless and eternal, possessing a preeminent excellence that is not of human origin.
In the communication of Viṣṇu’s majesty and regarding the true object of knowledge,
the scriptures and all the Purāṇas are the means of proof, being of human origin.
The Vedas were composed by Hari and the divine sages according to their true meanings;
they are eternal in substance, yet appear non-eternal due to the application of phonemes and word order.
The Sāttvika Purāṇas as well as the Smṛtis of Manu and others are indeed authoritative;
those devoted to Śrī Hari should accept what is stated therein as the truth.
"The Vārāha, Vaiṣṇava, Pādma, Vāyuprokta, Gāruḍa, and the Śrīmadbhāgavata are indeed the Sāttvika Purāṇas; such is the sacred tradition. (PS 1.4.32)
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Brahmavaivarta, the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Vāmana, the Bhaviṣya, and the Nārasiṃha—these six indeed belong to the quality of rajas. (PS 1.4.33)
The wise know that the Mātsya, Kaurmya, Laiṅgya, Śaiva, Skānda, and that which is called Pāśupata are the Tāmasa [Purāṇas]. (PS 1.4.34)
Everything spoken by the Sāttvika [authorities] is to be accepted, whether according to their specific applications or otherwise;
however, when there is a contradiction with the Vedas or the Vedānusāras, one should interpret it as having another meaning. (PS 1.4.35)
The other Purāṇas, which are contradictory and even produced from deception and delusion, as well as all those spoken by Vyāsa that are classified as Sāttvika, [are likewise rejected].
In some places, even those Purāṇas that generally produce knowledge have been spoken by others in infinite numbers due to the influence of possession by Asuras. (PS 1.4.37)
These [elements], though imperceptible to the ear, truly exist as immeasurable;
they are always proclaimed by the three supreme Śukras solely by the command of Viṣṇu.
Excessive sizes [of objects] are perceived due to the absence of possession by demons, ignorance, and so forth;
deafness and other such defects of the hearer are absent in those whose sense faculties are free from such flaws. (PS 1.4.39)
These objects of sense they say should be heard thousands of times;
being free from defects of sound, they are to be grasped along with the mind.
Therein, one should know the Lord Viṣṇu—the eternal, the goal, the truth, consisting of bliss and consciousness, free from defects, and endowed with infinite excellent qualities. (PS 1.4.41)
Indeed, by worshipping Hari, the Lord of the Self, with devotion, people become liberated;
they should possess the wisdom that recognizes the evil paths described in false scriptures as things to be abandoned.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"There are five organs of knowledge and five organs of action."
Among those [beings] who have reached the stage of the subtle element of earth, the ear alone is distinguished as being preeminent.
Because it is the means of accomplishment for the first offering of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it is superior in quality;
it resides pervading the entire body within the sphere of the skin and the flesh. (PS 1.5.2)
Leprosy (kuṣṭha), scabies (bhaṅgura), ringworm (pāmā), and so forth are proclaimed as skin disorders (tvak-doṣa);
they are unmanifest at first, free from defects of touch, and preceded by sensations of cold and heat. (PS 1.5.3)
Tangible objects are said to be their respective domains: air, fire, water, and earth; certain substances and qualities are the objects of the sense of touch. (PS 1.5.4)
Skin and touch are two principles established in primordial nature (prakṛti); they are eternal yet gross and non-eternal.
Those produced from them, which depend upon air (vāyu), are considered to be derived from nature (prākṛta) and perishable.

The objects of the sense-faculties are proclaimed to be mere constituents of the qualities (guṇamātrāḥ). All of those, belonging to that which is of the nature of cognition, are declared to be of two kinds. (PS 1.5.6)

Those [dreams] which are favorable for the service of Viṣṇu and his devotees are considered auspicious; those which are unfavorable are inauspicious. Furthermore, they are considered to be of three kinds.

Those who rely on what is fit for liberation are eternal; those who rely on what is fit for darkness are base; and those in between rely on what is fit for the eternal cycle, through their respective excellent means of accomplishment.
The mind, the vital breath, and the senses— which constitute the very nature of the individual soul— attain low, middling, and superior states through sequential application.
Their essential natures are eternal; among them, those in the highest [state] are also auspicious.
Those who are fit for liberation are the highest, while those who are eternally bound are the middling.

But those who are inferior are fit for darkness; likewise, those consisting of mind alone and so forth, as well as those possessing their own forms, those residing in the subtle body, and those dwelling in the gross body, are impermanent. (PS 1.5.11)
In Viṣṇu, in Māyā, in Brahmā and the others, and in those liberated through the gradual yoga,
there exist mind, the senses, cognition, happiness, fortitude, strength, and so forth.
The very forms of Viṣṇu are eternally pervasive in their entirety;
they are independent, as are the actions of the Great Self, the independent Person.
For one who is clearly established in his own true nature, there is no dependence on anything else regarding knowledge, action, or indeed all activities and forms. (PS 1.5.14)
He is declared to be independent; he is Viṣṇu and none other anywhere, for even the Self is devoid of a body composed of the unmanifest and its effects.
But those which consist of the faculties of the mind alone are eternal, all-pervading, and identical with their own nature;
they are under the sole control of Viṣṇu, for their existence indeed depends upon Hari.

Because it is dependent upon another, it is proclaimed to be non-independent; even for those beginning with Brahmā, whether liberated or unliberated, this lack of independence has existed from time immemorial.
The nature, knowledge, and activity of those whose minds are increasingly sublime are clearly established as being progressively higher or lower. (PS 1.5.18)
For from grace proceed all things, such as knowledge, devotion, and so forth;
as well as the liberation from the darkness of ignorance and knowledge, and [the realization of] the eternal, the non-eternal, and the insentient. (PS 1.5.19)
The birth and destruction of all three kinds of living beings occur entirely preceded by their own nature, suffering, hatred, envy, anxiety, and torment. (PS 1.5.20)
For those who are liberated, there is no connection with a body as long as fear and so forth persist;
and even when they do occur, such as fear and the like, they arise only from those who are suitable [to cause them], and only in a very slight degree among the most excellent.
Knowledge and liberation are not seen even in a dream by those who are unfit; nor do they ever exist for the fit, as long as the darkness of ignorance regarding their own true nature persists.
The wise know that the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this world, as well as destiny, knowledge, ignorance, darkness, and liberation, are all brought about by Viṣṇu alone.
The essential nature of Brahmā and the others is considered to be exceedingly subtle;
their sense organs are likewise subtle, yet they are indeed stable. (PS 1.5.24)
The eye is located in the eyeball; it is the grasper of form and is beyond the senses.
It is eternal when residing in its unmanifest state, gross, non-eternal when produced, and is the organ of sight. (PS 1.5.25)
The two eyes, both eternal and non-eternal, are fashioned by the eye of one's own nature;
they bestow knowledge, are designated as witnesses, and are the sense-organ for the essential form of all things.
Of the sense-faculties already mentioned and those yet to be described, taken collectively,
no power exists without the assistance of their own essential forms as sense-faculties.
Through its qualities and defects, it experiences increase and decrease according to its own nature;
yet the witness-consciousness, being the observer of the fit [faculties], remains so except for its betrayal of its own superior.

Even in that case, it may be slightly obstructed by something; all of that [obstruction] consists of cataracts, jaundice, opacities of the lens, the reflection of light, or the convergence of rays. (PS 1.5.29)
Eye diseases, wounds and the like, as well as those caused by obstructed bile, such as the whirling of the eyes and coldness, are proclaimed to be the defects of the eyes. (PS 1.5.30)
Being too near, being too far, subtlety, obstruction, similarity, and equal impact are proclaimed as defects of the object. (PS 1.5.31)
Those which are the objects of description and those which are the range of the vision of description—
white, red, white-yellow, green, and so forth, in their entirety.
Colors such as variegated and others are the intrinsic natures and objects of the eye;
they consist of fire, water, and earth, and are conjoined with manifest color-form.
Some say that the objects of the eye are the rising sun and the immortals;
others declare the tongue, residing in its bulbous base, to be the supreme sense organ of taste.
Beyond the senses are lack of relish and so forth; its defects are eruptions and the like; and there are the bitter, pungent, astringent, salty, sweet, and sour tastes.
Likewise, "variegated flavor" (citrarasa) and so forth are the objects of the gustatory faculty;
they clearly produce the cognition of flavor in one who is free from defects. (PS 1.5.36)
It quickly generates knowledge that is natural and established in its own nature;
whereas tastes that are spoiled, stale, deficient in potency, or putrid are harmful. (PS 1.5.37)
The tongue, when in contact with tastes, is not devoid of defects and thus does not grant knowledge;
for objects on the ground are subject to disease and fall within the range of the gustatory faculty.
The powerful olfactory faculty is said to reside in the nasal cavity;
diseases such as chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) are defects of the nose, and it is considered the sense organ for perceiving odors.
Those beginning with "mixed" (vyāmiśra) are declared to be portions of defects, specifically the defects of odor;
that which resides in the mouth-ball (vaktragolaka) is called the sense-organ of speech, which is beyond the reach of the senses.
His words may be eternal or non-eternal, true or false,
logical or illogical, and they may be in the refined language of the gods (Sanskrit) or in the vernacular.

Muteness and other such major defects, as well as qualities within the range of speech that are free from them—such as stammering and indistinctness—are proclaimed to be the defects of speech. (PS 1.5.42)
They say that the sense-organ of the hand is located in the ball of the hand and is supersensible;
its defects, such as being three fingers long, are absent in the [other] sense-organs, which are therefore faultless.
For one always takes for oneself what is beneficial both here and in the next world;
therefore, objects such as land, gems, gold, and so forth, are considered to have great value.
Furthermore, such entities as stones are considered objects of the hands;
thorns, food remnants, pebbles, scorpions, and the like are sources of undesirable sensation.

Objects that are to be abandoned should always be considered as things to be relinquished with both hands; likewise, that which brings about what is undesirable is considered harmful for the hands, while that which is beneficial is considered a source of benefit for them.
The wise declare that the excrement residing in the balls of the feet is the impurity of the organ of the feet;
lameness and other such conditions are defects of the feet, while the means for achieving faultless movement [is purity].
That which pertains to one's own nature, that which pertains to primordial matter, and that which is derived from primordial matter—this is considered the threefold [nature].
By whichever sense organ whatever action is always performed by the virtuous, [that is its specific function].
That is declared to be its object; it is the domain of the sense organ named after that [object].
It consists of what is digested and undigested, what has been eaten, and the wind located in the stomach.
That which is the opposite of timely is called *śakṛt* by the wise; the evacuation of such matter is declared to be the domain of the anus. (PS 1.5.50)

Fistula-in-ano and other such primary ulcers located in the anus, as well as the humors (doṣas) causing constipation or diarrhea, do not perform their function if they are situated in the rectum. (PS 1.5.51)

The female and male sexual organs, such as the vulva and the penis, located within the body and beyond the reach of the senses, are designated by the two terms "upastha" and "śiśna"; these two organs are free from defects.
The two [semen and blood] are considered to be the substrates for pleasure and procreation;
they are the basis for urine, wounds, and other such defects, while that which is free from defects accomplishes its own purpose.
That which is both primary (prakṛta) and derivative (prākṛta), endowed with its own nature and sense-faculties, is indeed capable of purposeful action; it certainly cannot be otherwise. (PS 1.5.54)
All five organs of cognition and the five organs of action are characterized by passion (rajas), possess the capacity for discernment, and are endowed with distinct powers.
The objects of the sense organs are considered to be sound and the rest, in their respective order;
these—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are regarded as qualities (guṇas). 1.56.

The wise say that the elements, which consist of the subtle constituents (*mātrā*) and are delimited by them, exist within the womb as the internal essence of the five gross elements; thus the elements are merged within the embryos.
The pentad residing within ignorance in the form of existence, containing the womb of the qualities,
is the pentad of existents established within the elements merged in the measures (mātrās).
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmiśra, and andhatāmisra—these they call the states of darkness; moha is considered to reside in sound. (PS 1.5.59)
Great delusion resides in form; darkness resides in taste; that which is called blind darkness resides in smell—these are the forms of the afflictions.
These [subtle elements] existing in their primordial state are eternal and most minute;
however, they declare that the gross elements manifested as actual beings are non-eternal.
The nature of the individual soul (jīva) is not distinct from that [Supreme Self], even when residing in the subtle body (liṅgadeha);
it is proclaimed to be the concealer of the true knowledge of the soul's own nature.

Because it brings about that [ignorance], darkness is an obstacle to the knowledge of the true nature of things; it causes one to proceed toward what is contrary to the knowledge of their true nature. (PS 1.5.63)
That delusion which does not cease even upon receiving instruction is great delusion; they say that hostility toward instructors is "darkness. (PS 1.5.64)
Beginningless ignorance is said to be the sole cause of profound nescience, characterized by false reasoning and the inaccessible, and designated as "blinding darkness."
Since beginningless time, there have been infinite and boundless atoms;
indeed, those whose nature is as minute as a hair-tip or the like, numbering tens of thousands, constitute the objective domain of the self.

They are protected at the time of dissolution and created [again] at the time of emanation by Hari, who takes the form of the sun's orb according to their respective natures and forms, and who is eternally inseparable from them.

For those beings who exist at the beginning of this kalpa and so forth, within their respective kalpas, the created beings are of three kinds by nature: distinct, similar, and dissimilar, occurring in due order.

All living beings, from time immemorial, are devoid of independence and are subject to Ramā; bound by the subtle body (liṅga) consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti), they reside within the womb of Śrī Hari.

At the time of creation, Hari created beings both outside and inside the cosmic egg; those within were composed of sattva and were of low, middling, and high [qualities], while those outside were not composed of the [pure] principles.
All those preceded by the partless, the immortals, and the gandharvas are like blades of grass;
they are fit for the eternal flow, and all those fit for darkness as well.
All those living beings who are connected to a *liṅga* are not otherwise;
they too, through their own appropriate means of accomplishment, [attained this state] in previous infinite kalpas.
Those who are liberated, those who are middling, and those who have attained darkness—all reside within the womb of Śrī Hari;
by the decree of Hari, there shall never be any completion for them anywhere at any time.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"When the measure of the night has passed entirely, at the arrival of the following day..."
In that moment, the all-powerful Lord himself desired to create that [universe], the creator of the universe.
Then the Lord, having released the living beings residing within his own womb from their subtle bodies (liṅga),
enveloped them in three ways with a body consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The Lord, known by the name Puruṣa, having extracted from within his own belly those beings who were differentiated as consisting of tamas, rajas, and sattva, brought them forth.
The Lord of the World, together with the one called Vāsudeva, bestowed [this knowledge] upon all living beings;
yet there is no creation at all for those who are liberated, nor indeed for those who are bound in every respect.
Emission has been described; it is now stated that emission is governed by numerical restriction.
Emission, through the restriction of number, occurs among both the real and the unreal. (PS 1.6.5)
In partless entities there is no number; because it consists of multiplicity, it exists only as manifold.
There are infinite groups called "straight" who are fit for the state of Brahman. (PS 1.6.6)
Among them, indeed, there are those who have been liberated infinitely many times over from previous endless kalpas;
yet there are also those bound by the subtle body (liṅga), existing within the womb in infinite-infinite numbers.
O Hari, let all of them be created by You; yet among them, let some be those who are upright and so forth, being real and having been directly perceived since beginningless time.
Indeed, those who perceive their respective objects directly— both generally and specifically—
do so by means of great instruments appropriate to the time prescribed for them.
For those who are upright strive for the direct realization of the goal, numbering one hundred;
and those who perceive both the prior and the subsequent are always numbered at one hundred as well.
Even those who always strive for the worship of Hari’s infinite qualities as proclaimed in the Vedas,
gradually come to worship the entire collection of His attributes.
In this world, those who possess the practice of complete and virtuous qualities become perfected beings;
they indeed become liberated in due course, for liberation does not occur all at once.
And thus, by means of two hundred Brahma-measures of time,
she whose power is complete and whose worship of qualities is perfect becomes fully liberated.
O gods, in the moment immediately preceding liberation, and even when the well-initiated prārabdha karma that is to be experienced has been exhausted,
the number [of moments] is likewise fixed in the same way hereafter as well.
The sons of the Unborn (Aja) are liberated by the kalpas to be described hereafter;
however, the remaining ones, beginning with Śeṣa, together with their wives, are measured by fifty-two kalpas.
The *indrajīva*s last for twenty kalpas; those of the *ahaṃ* and *prāṇa* categories last for eighteen kalpas; and the *guru* and others last for twelve kalpas. (PS 1.6.16)
The flow [of the yugas] lasts for twelve kalpas; the sun and the other [planets] have a duration of ten kalpas;
that of Mitra and the others is nine [kalpas]; and for the remaining group, it has been stated [to be eight].
For the group beginning with Sanaka and others, it is by eight times seven kalpas;
for the group beginning with Parjanya and ending with Puṣkara, it is indeed by six [kalpas].

The karma-devas perceive directly for five kalpas; those born of noble birth perceive directly through four [kalpas], while those born of magical creation perceive directly for three and a half kalpas.
For the gopīs through contact with Kṛṣṇa’s body, for the host of ancestors through three kalpas,
for the gandharvas through two kalpas, and likewise for mortals through one.
For those worthy ones who behold Hari, the period of restriction lasts for half a kalpa;
this rule remains exactly thus throughout all kalpas and not otherwise.
The number of kalpas is to be understood by those with discerning minds according to the measure of Brahmā;
the attainment of darkness by the asuras occurs at the end of a day and a kalpa of Brahmā.
The command of the Sustainer of the World is indeed always thus:
[He ordains] for those beginning with Indra and ending with Puṣkara, according to what is appropriate for their cultivation of qualities.
They are liberated by the aforementioned eons; however, the practice [of meditation] must first be performed for as many eons until direct perception [arises]. This is the certainty. (PS 1.6.24)
As long as Brahmā, arisen from a lotus, remains within the interior of the cosmic egg, for that long he exists even throughout every single day of the years that have passed.

All these [attainments] are partial and not ultimate; however, according to the number that will be stated, those who abide in the stages and possess direct perception are measured as such even in every eon.
The Apsarases, beginning with Urvaśī and numbering up to a hundred, are measured by a count of eight;
they are equal to those born from the navel [of Brahmā] and are similar to the highest Karmadevas.
Among the ancestors, there are one hundred and seven who are equal to Urvaśī and others;
others are inferior to those born of noble lineage, and from them, they are progressively lower in rank.
Among them, there are one hundred Gandharvas, eight of whom are equal in merit born of their actions;
all the Ṛṣis number one hundred crores, with twenty being the most excellent.
It is declared that a hundred sages are equal to the gods by action;
among them, twenty who are possessed by Hari are slightly superior in merit.
Among those very [beings], eight hundred are real, equal to those born of karma;
the others, even though they are sons of Agni, are equal to those born of ignorance.
There are eighteen thousand and thirty Cāraṇas and Rākṣasas;
likewise, there are seventy others among all the [divine] classes, such as the Sādhyas and Siddhas.
Those born of noble birth are not inferior; they are joined with the Pitṛs and Gandharvas.
Those who rely on external signs possess parts, while those inferior to them are partless.
Among them, those who take hold of the *pratīka* [the opening words of a verse] are the best; the human singers (*mānuṣagāyaka*) are superior to them;
the kings are inferior to those, and the mortal-born (*martyocca*) are lower still.
Among all the multitudes of living beings, from the mortal world and the hosts of gandharvas upwards,
all those who are fit for liberation rely upon the support of a representative image (pratīka).
Before direct perception, they are partless; even after [perception], they remain within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
For once they are created, they possess parts and are devoid of direct perception.

But for those who have direct perception, whose parts are real, and whose minds are distinct from [the unreal], there is karma and so forth; for those who lack such reality, there are gods, gandharvas, and humans. (PS 1.6.37)

The attainment of the subtle state for these beings who have reached the end of their lives occurs through non-obstruction; it is certain that the attainment of the gross state occurred within the cosmic egg prior to the birth of the Unborn.
For those who are real [beings], the attainment of subtle and gross forms is held to occur outside the cosmic egg;
prior to the emergence of the egg, those gods possessed bodies that were uncombined [with matter]. (PS 1.6.39)

Within the interior of the cosmic egg, all those possessing gross bodies are intermingled; indeed, at the time of dissolution, all those bound to their subtle bodies dwell within the womb of the void.
Among those, the non-liberated are considered to be created according to a fixed number;
and Vāsudeva undertook to create all of them.
The primordial nature (prakṛti), known as the insentient, is the subtle body (liṅga) for all living beings;
the souls residing within the womb of that nature are considered to be endowed with the subtle body.
Since beginningless time, living beings have been subject to the bondage of saṃsāra;
therein, in a previous infinite aeon, those beings [attained it] through the practice of the true means.
And there were three kinds of living beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, whose bonds were not yet severed due to their mixed or perverted knowledge.
Among those to be created who are bound by their subtle bodies (liṅga), the four-faced Brahmā is the first to be created;
and the creation of all does not occur at one and the same time, due to the difference in time.
Therefore, those born earlier are superior, while others are inferior;
this occurs when the period known as dissolution (laya), at the end of supreme time, has passed and creation is recognized to have begun.
The creation of these [elements] from primordial time belongs to the Unborn (Aja); the creation of another is from time;
and after the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Vāyu occurs after a hundred years.
Then, for a hundred years, there was the speech of Bhāratī; for another hundred years from that, and then for a thousand years, there was the creation of the two, Vipra and Śeṣa.
Then, after a thousand years for each [stage] beginning with Nīla, and likewise for that same duration for the others; thereafter, however, it is ten thousand years for Vāruṇī and the rest.
The creation of Indra and Kāma lasts for ten thousand years, and likewise others;
and those who were created by Hari as inferior beings are surpassed by the most excellent of all.
Those ending with Puṣkara are real, and likewise others are unreal;
they are partless, eternally bound, and fit for darkness—these are the Rākṣasas.
After ten thousand years according to the divine reckoning, through the established order of each preceding period, creation occurs;
that [creation] is considered to be twofold, distinguished as subtle and gross.
For all those who are established in their true state and have attained direct realization, [the creation] occurs prior to the cosmic egg; for others, it occurs within it.
Furthermore, for the beings being born both outside the cosmic egg and within the cosmic egg,
creation is to be understood as occurring in due order according to the previously stated temporal restrictions.
But when the attainment of the subtle body by one bound to the *liṅga* is desired,
then, in the preceding moment, a disturbance of the qualities (*guṇavaiṣamya*) is held to exist within that *liṅga*.
The portion of passion (rajas) situated in the center of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) is proclaimed [as the earth];
there, the one named Bhū is Indirā, who is his proud mistress (māninī).
At the time of the dissolution of the ten [worlds], however, the rajasic atoms that were adjacent to the sattvic earth become adjacent to the sattva itself. (PS 1.6.57)
At the end of the time of dissolution, they all abide there;
the rajasic atom, having entered the sattvic portion, remains there individually and separately.
These ten such [atoms], when combined, become twelve atoms;
they are fully capable of producing one hundred red-colored [atoms] within the sattvic [beings].
By their very nature, those sattva-components are white and established as sattva;
those numbering one thousand are red, consisting of ten rajas-atoms.
And when touched by *rajas*, they go toward *sattva* during dissolution; likewise, a single *rājasa* atom moves counter-clockwise toward the portions of *rajas*.
The portion of tamas brought from the earth, being its own hundredth part and exceedingly small,
makes that [portion] dark blue and renders it intensely red.
One part is pure and the other is rajasic;
yet even when they abide in the middle state or during dissolution, these two remain equal to the rajasic atom.
Those *tāmasa* atoms which have reached the state of being delimited by darkness are such; while in dissolution, the *rājasa* atoms are situated alongside the delimitation of *sattva*. (PS 1.6.64)
These twelve atoms (aṇus) that have thus combined are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa); they are rajasic and extremely minute in size, being only slightly larger than a single atom.
There, multiplied further, there are twelve hundred Sāttvika atoms, joined with ten Rajas atoms.
For these indeed become useful for practical purposes;
however, the rajasic [discrimination] is held to be twice as great as the tamasic discrimination.
The sattvic [perception] is held to be twice the size of the rājasic unit;
moreover, within each single unit, there are infinite atoms.
There dwell the controllers, consisting of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva;
Nārāyaṇa, who possesses infinite qualities, and Śrī, who takes pride in the form of a woman.

In primordial nature (prakṛti), which is insentient, and likewise in the subtle body (liṅgadeha), there exist infinite individual souls (aṇu); among them, those previously mentioned are the ones who accomplish their tasks.

They say that the portions characterized by passion (rājasāṃśa) when associated with goodness (sattvaṅgata) lead to dissolution; those associated with darkness (tāmasagata) consist of passion, goodness, and darkness (rajo-rāja-sat-tāmasa).
The wise say that when the *rajas* has reached its limit and becomes *rājasa* and *tāmasa*, there is indeed dissolution (*laya*) through the will of the illustrious Hari. (PS 1.6.72)
The wise call this state of equilibrium the condition of primordial nature (prakṛti) and its marks (liṅga).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"The subtle body (liṅgadeha) is shaped like a coconut fruit and is considered to be threefold."
It is always provided with an aperture at the crown of the head and contains the space of the womb.
Those living beings, though of three kinds, are bound within; they are not capable of liberation, for they dwell fully within the apertures at the top of Rāmā’s head.
Those bound by gender are touched by suffering, whereas those who are truly liberated are untouched by suffering;
for it is by Viṣṇu that one’s subtle destruction occurs at the improper time.
By Aniruddha, that [subtle body] is gradually cast out from within to the exterior;
in the subsequent moment, the state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmyatā) occurs in the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
That [state], which consists of the knowledge of one's own true nature, becomes obscured by the stages of existence (bhūmi) and obstructs the knowledge of living beings;
meanwhile, the efforts and desires of the virtuous are directed toward the bliss of the knowledge of one's own nature during the dissolution [of worldly states].
In a state of equilibrium they remain obstructed, but in disequilibrium they quickly attain manifestation;
indeed, these two states occur in the linga sequentially during dissolution and creation.
As they revolve moment by moment, he [perceives] that [wheel] revolving to the left and otherwise;
this occurs through the excellent conjunction of the three qualities (guṇas) residing within the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
At the time of creation, the intellect of living beings is held to be divided threefold:
as *sāttvikī*, *rājasī*, and *tāmasī* in their entirety.
Among the fit, sattvic intellect is abundant; others hold it to be meager. But among middling beings, the mind is rajasic or tamasic. (PS 1.7.9)

Gradually, while [the knowledge] will exist in others in a much greater measure, it will exist in only a very small measure in two; the fivefold ignorance residing in the subtle body (liṅgadeha) arises from the five [categories] beginning with the gross elements.
That which is designated as beginningless ignorance is external and devoid of its own nature;
for it arises when the witness [self] is joined with the mind through the senses by means of *tamas*. (PS 1.7.11)

If there is a conjunction of the witness-consciousness with the senses and the mind established in sattva, then here, for the three types of consciousness, there arises external knowledge of their own respective forms. (PS 1.7.12)
If there is a conjunction of the senses with the mind through passion, then that which is external, unreal in nature, and characterized by desire, anger, and so forth [arises]. (PS 1.7.13)
If the faculties of knowledge were limited by the quality of *rajas*, there would be an endless desire for the three kinds of living beings. (PS 1.7.14)

The desire for external objects such as sound, which is conjoined with the witness-consciousness and the senses, is called "beginningless desire" (anādikāma) here among the three types of consciousnesses. (PS 1.7.15)
If the faculties of action, having reached the state of being delimited by *rajas*, are joined with the witness-faculty (*sākṣin*), they produce even beginningless karma. (PS 1.7.16)
Action is considered to reside in the subtle body (liṅga), but not in its own essential nature;
beginningless ignorance and desire, as well as beginningless action, reside in the subtle body.
But thinking "this is mine," the conscious being becomes bound, even though it has obtained human birth in the land of Bhārata over time. (PS 1.7.18)

Having attained the state of a Brahmin, the company of a true guru, and the realization of devotion and knowledge through the grace of Śrī Hari, one should then perform the rites for the deities within [the heart].
Outside the egg, by the will of Hari, Śrī Bhagavān dwells in the Vaikuṇṭha palace situated beyond the cosmic boundary,
touching the shell of the egg.
Just as water, having been submerged while situated around the outermost circumference of a vessel,
[remains there], so it is for existing things whose true nature has become manifest when there is a reversal of their marks (liṅga).

In the mortal birth in Bhārata, the two monkeys (the senses) were driven away from the egg by hatred toward the enemy (the mind), resulting in the destruction of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) within the egg due to the increase of bad association. (PS 1.7.22)
Through the blow of the mace of mindfulness, the unwholesome perishes by the application of time;
likewise, beginningless ignorance and desire, as well as beginningless karma, are destroyed.
Therefore, ignorance and the like are not proclaimed to be external to their own nature;
for knowledge and ignorance reside in their own nature, being neither eternal nor transitory.
When the state of equilibrium occurs regarding beginningless ignorance, desire, and so forth, then for every individual soul (jīva), these never arise again.

In dissolution, the tamaḥ-atom possesses the luster of two hundredths of a rajas-atom; when those [tamas-atoms] dissolve, there remains one rajas-atom, and ten [atoms] belonging to the side of sattva.
When darkness (tamas) alone exists in the middle, it remains fixed;
when a particle of passion (rajas) enters that existing darkness, it becomes twice as much rajas.
The tamasic atoms present within the sattvic [state] possess a luster equal to a hundredth part of a hundredth of a rajasic atom;
indeed, they certainly dissolve into the sattvic atoms that are ten times superior even to those [rajasic ones].
In this way, they cause [the qualities] to become blue; thus is this state of equilibrium proclaimed.
This state of equilibrium is considered to be twofold: tamasic and rajasic. (PS 1.7.29)
Indeed, a state of equilibrium never exists in the *sāttvika* [state] alone;
rather, it is through two states of equilibrium that the characteristic of a person is determined. (PS 1.7.30)
The wise declare that sleep is the destruction of everything;
when there is a cessation of the desire for yoga, then the Lord makes himself known.
The desire for what is unfit and the effort [to achieve it] cut off the agent's hope;
for when there is a discrepancy in the indicative sign (liṅga), the desire to procreate indeed arises.
Whenever a desire arises in a living being, then the Lord creates him—
among all beings to be created— either outside the cosmic egg or within the chariot.
For the uneven states of the goats and other [beings] do not occur simultaneously;
rather, they arise sequentially, according to their prior measure, both inside and outside the cosmic egg.

The state of equilibrium belongs to the base ones, while that of the superior one occurs before and after; those rajasic atoms which have entered into sattva during dissolution are the ten [faculties]. (PS 1.7.35)
At the time of creation, indeed, the atoms, endowed with their own hundred and more constituent qualities, enter into the portion of *rajas* when impelled by *śrī*.
When the Rajasic atom, which had reached the state of delimitation within darkness, dissolves,
it takes up a hundredth part of its own Tamasic atom, impelled by Durgā.
When the time for creation has arrived, they enter the portion of *rajas*;
at the time of dissolution, the atom belonging to the *rājasa* [nature] remains within the portion of *rajas*.
Rajas manifests itself in the middle when the time for creation has arrived;
likewise, if such is the state of the qualities, so too does the subtle body [manifest] within primordial nature.
The wise have declared this to be the state of equilibrium; from it, creation will come into being.
At the time of dissolution, those ten tamasic atoms (aṇu) which have entered into sattva—// PS_1,7.40 //
Those [atoms] which possess the luster of a hundredth part of a rajasic atom, when joined with sattvic atoms equal to themselves,
enter the tamasic portion, as declared by Śrī.
A particle of darkness (tāmasāṇu) joined with passion (rajas), when itself balanced by a prior particle of goodness (sattva),
[arises] from its own [nature] and from goodness.
It is indeed conjoined with twice as many rajasic atoms.
Remaining there during the period of dissolution, when the time for creation arrives once more,
they are impelled by the earth and enter the portion of darkness by the will of Śrī Hari.
A single pure *tāmasa* atom [is formed] by the previous *tāmasa* and *sāttvika* atoms;
likewise, a *rājasatāmasa* [atom is formed] by ten [atoms] including one *tāmasa*. (PS 1.7.44)
Having reached and merged with that which is called the inequality of darkness (tamas), all [the atoms] combine:
ten rājasa atoms with one thousand sāttvika atoms.
When the subtle atom (aṇu), which is pure and associated with a single quality of rajas, becomes united with tamas, that state of imbalance is called rajas. (PS 1.7.46)
From the imbalance of *rajas* comes creation; from the imbalance of *tamas* comes dissolution.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"When the time of dissolution has passed and the time of creation has arrived,"
But at the beginning of another time-cycle and so forth, the Puruṣa [creates] all sentient beings.

Within the body of Vāsudeva, he [creates] individual souls (jīvas) bound to their respective limiting adjuncts (liṅgas), who are diverse, possessed of varying degrees of excellence, and endowed with capacities according to their own fitness.

Beholding those who, through their respective actions, were intent upon great efforts appropriate to themselves and were situated in the state of Vāsudeva as befitting their attainment of birth, he reflected.

For that [unmanifest], which is bound by the subtle body appropriate for the unblinking [state] at the beginning of the time of creation and so forth, is indeed joined with the heterogeneity of the preceding moment. (PS 1.8.4)
Having taken one [breath], the omnipresent Saṅkarṣaṇa bestowed other living beings;
he took that single breath into his own subtle body (liṅga), and from it, other conscious beings.
Pradyumna gave his two wives to those two, taking them along with their insignia;
