he [then] appointed others as officiating priests (ārtvijas) for all the ritual stations, having consecrated them as such.

To those who had directly perceived the Manifested, the Lord of All, Aniruddha, in accordance with the rule of number and through subtle yoga, bestowed the power to create, beginning from the last [element] up to the end.
Vāsudeva agitated the subtle body (liṅgadeha) of Viriñca; from the three qualities residing within that subtle body, three drops emerged.
Whatever drop of the *sattva* quality fell there was pure;
likewise, a drop of *rajas*, joined with an imbalance of *rajas*, fell down. (PS 1.8.9)
Then, from that, the drop of *tamas* became possessed of the imbalance of *tamas*;
and Viṣṇu, having entered the drop of *rajas*, [became] the powerful imbalance of *rajas*.
Having set aside the pure drop of *rajas*, the Teacher of the World [placed] the Lord within the wheel of the drop of *tamas*; that was the intense imbalance of *tamas*.
Having extracted and set it aside separately, he made that drop pure;
then Vāsudeva, the primordial one, was entreated by Māyā.
The omnipresent Lord, though unborn, is bound by the signs of the imbalance of the quality of *rajas*;
for the sake of the unborn soul’s acquisition of a subtle body, there is a powerful imbalance of *rajas*.
Having cast it into Māyā and swallowed that which is called the Great (mahat),
Hari deposited that subtle form of the primordial potency (vīrya) within her.
There she gave birth to the unborn, all-pervading one who possesses a subtle body;
previously, the atoms of the three qualities remained fixed according to the rule of Sāṃkhya.
As many as those [atoms] are, they are always eternal; their destruction is not found.
Therein, all the atoms of sentient beings are perpetually accumulated in ten ways.
The atoms belonging to the Rajas and Tamas qualities exist by virtue of a quarter-measure;
they become accumulated as subtle entities moving within the wind, the Sarasvatī, and so forth.
For the ten qualities, beginning with existence (*satva*), arise in a state of intense power;
indeed, they prevail as superior [states] even over subtle things such as grass and the like. (PS 1.8.18)
For the atoms of living beings, as well as those consisting of passion (rājas) and darkness (tāmasa), arise from the subtle atoms of the upright, accumulated by the feet. 1.8.19.
In all composite subtle bodies that possess parts, the atoms of sentient beings undergo an increase of tenfold in their accumulation. (PS 1.8.20)
In those who are very high or slightly low, the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* predominate;
taking hold of that imbalance of the *rajas* quality, the first-born [Brahmā] himself became the younger brother [Viṣṇu].
At the end of all subtle bodies, that which causes destruction dwells;
it is composed of sattva, rajas, and tamas, and has the nature of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva.
The Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā, who possesses infinite forms, assumes the names Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña, appearing as white, red, and blue respectively.
Hari, residing in the three locations within each respective subtle body, [manifests] those three states; indeed, due to His specific distinctions therein, these [states] are blissful.
The two faces with nineteen apertures are named Viśva and Taijasa;
they are situated on the right and left respectively, while the face of Puruṣa is in the middle.
Moreover, the function of her faces is like that of elephants;
Viśva resides in the right eye, established in sattva, having attained the portion of sattva.
Through the three gates consisting of sattva, [the mind] perceives the state called waking for those who consider themselves superior, middling, or inferior. (PS 1.8.27)
Indeed, that very [power] called "the middle" acts through a triad upon those who are high,
middling, and low— namely gods, humans, and slaves— during the state known as waking.
For he alone, by means of his three internal mouths, brings about the various states;
indeed, he is the activator of the partless individual souls while they are awake.
In this way, for men, [the consequences] will be through those who speak from the left; and for women, it will be likewise.
But these are the deeds performed by the vast mortal bodies throughout infinite and endless births.
In the state of waking, those vocal expressions made by the mind and the senses—whether sattvic and so forth, and whether high or low—are called *karmāṇi*. (PS 1.8.31)
Whatever all those various thoughts may be,
when they have perished, their unperceived traces remain fully present.
Indeed, those things given for enjoyment perish after being consumed;
and those given for enjoyment remain half-consumed in every respect.
Among those very [karmas], some *prārabdha* ones undergo exhaustion through experience;
it is clear that once direct realization (*aparokṣa*) has occurred, only the remaining *prārabdha* karma persists.
And not all [karmas] that are fit for experience lead [to fruition], without a doubt;
among them, the Unborn (the Lord) brings about much or little [result] from that which has arisen from a bad beginning.
Indeed, such is the will of Hari through the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One, that infinite objects for the enjoyment of living beings have not been granted by Hari. (PS 1.8.36)
Even those karmic impressions residing in the *liṅga*, which have been accumulated here by the millions and gathered into a heap, become clearly manifest when there is direct perception.
Even those who have been burned or destroyed certainly do not exist; there is no doubt that mortals live here in this Bhārata for thousands of millions of times.
Bound and powerless, he performs these actions by his very nature an infinite number of times,
throughout infinite births for a duration of infinite and boundless lifespans.
The dissolution of accumulated karmas occurs through the experience of their fruits;
even over infinite and vast periods of Brahmā’s time, there is no dissolution for some karmas that have not yet been experienced.
It is not possible for them to eat anywhere else; however, by the command of Hari, this fruit shall indeed belong to those living beings upon the sight of Śrī Viṣṇu.
Even though they have been written down again and again on leaves by Citraguptas,
the gods such as Ramā, Brahmā, and others remain presiding over all their respective actions.
Having torn up the written documents by the messengers of Yama with their own hands, Hari never yields to them any fruit of merit or evil at any time.
"O living being, even though [the karmic accumulation] awakens you, there is no fear for you from that which has been accumulated";
for this reason, they indeed declare the destruction of what has been accumulated.
The destruction of karmas is not at all praised as being like the destruction of a jar or similar objects;
rather, every well-initiated action is exhausted only through its experience.
But after that which is immediate, the virtuous declare that the action performed—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is called "the future"; thus, there will be no loss of what has been done.
O best of gods, Citragupta does not record those [deeds] on the scroll;
he grants them no fruit, and therefore people do not become attached.
And that [result] is undesirable because of future karmas; for kings indeed grasp at desirable meritorious acts, and thus they obtain what is desired. (PS 1.8.48)
The Kali age seizes those who harbor future hatred for Viṣṇu and the like, and no others;
one who is liberated through future devotion enjoys the bliss that is to be attained.

Even that which is declared in the Vedas may be as if not declared in the Vedas, depending on whether it is produced by knowledge or ignorance and so forth; likewise, it depends on whether it is performed in childhood, youth, or old age, and whether it is done through speech, body, or mind. (PS 1.8.50)
Whether performed out of fear, affection, or through possession, this person performs both auspicious and inauspicious actions while fully aware; being awake, he experiences their fruit. (PS 1.8.51)
Whether on the entire surface of the earth, in the cavities, or in the atmosphere;
in all worlds such as heaven, both inside and outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Whether in hell, in darkness, or in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms, a person, being always dependent on the Universe, experiences the fruit of their karma while awake. (PS 1.8.53)
They are established in Ānantāsana, Vaikuṇṭha, and Śvetadvīpa;
likewise in the worlds beginning with Mahar and ending with Satya, as well as outside the cosmic egg.
Those who are real [liberated ones] are restricted to their own respective offices, and not other people;
for all those who have realized the truth directly experience the fruit of their own prārabdha karma.
For those who are unreal and partless, there can never be eligibility for anything anywhere; and what need is there to speak of those who are unfit and merely experiencers of suffering? (PS 1.8.56)
The *riyu* attain the three worlds by means of action, and those beyond them solely through knowledge; among them, the foremost go to Hari, while the others go to Vāyu alone. (PS 1.8.57)
Those who are unripened do not go to Vāyu or to Hari;
remaining merely in their own place, they are indeed exempt from rebirth.
In the worlds accessible through knowledge— within the cosmic egg, from the Maharloka up to the end—
the sequence of elevation belongs to those who are unreal and partless, culminating in liberation.
Even for those who are truly without parts, their dwelling among the lowest of mortals in this creation will not be devoid of desire, owing to the merit they have previously undertaken.

It is taught that for those who possess reality, pleasure, pain, and so forth, arise from present merit and demerit, as well as from accumulated merit and demerit that have been assigned for experience.
For those who possess no merit and for those with little merit, residence in the wombs of animals is ordained;
for those with even less merit, residence in hell is intended. (PS 1.8.62)
For those who are qualified, there is no descent into darkness (tamas) resulting from either their prārabdha or their accumulated karma (sañcita);
however, for those who are unqualified, the attainment of darkness will occur through the ripening of their aversion.
Those ending with the Gandharvas of the gods are designated by the term "devas" in their respective order;
for the gods, there is no hell whatsoever, nor even darkness in any way.
Likewise, there is never liberation for the asuras by anyone, anywhere, at any time—
whether in the eight regions beginning with Bhārata, in the seven continents, or among the mountains.

For all beings, through the accumulation of primary *prārabdha* karma consisting of both sins and merits, darkness arises from the conjunction with false knowledge; [therefore] the state of Hari is attained by knowledge alone.
The fruit arising from those previously mentioned actions indeed belongs to the waking state.
That Viśva, who is the initiator of the waking state, becomes the one whose eye is the unborn [Ājāna]. (PS 1.8.67)
Having taken up the sattva arising from the subtle body (liṅga) and moving through its subtle state,
he has no accumulated bodily constituents, no objects of desire, and perceives no sin or the like.
There is no suffering from the onset of dejection, nor doubt or error; there is no evil desire, no discontent with others, no longing for sense-objects, and no harmful association. (PS 1.8.69)
There is no identification with the body, nor any movement of the body and senses toward the path of untruth;
there is constant delight in selfless action, true knowledge, and genuine devotion.
For by the grace of this supreme Brahman, there is constant happiness;
one should abandon that fruit of suffering preceded by dreams, sleep, and disease.
Sontaraṅga is considered by Hari himself to be his most excellent beloved;
he perceives Keśava directly through the remnants of the *pakva* offering and other such means. (PS 1.8.72)
Since beginningless time, the multitudes of living beings have always perceived Hari as befitting themselves through successive births, for the sake of direct realization.
Having seen the Lord, those who possess a hundred kalpas strive for the end of a hundred kalpas to attain that state through the worship of His qualities as proclaimed in the infinite Vedas.
Then, from Vāsudeva, there arose for him a subtle body; having taken up the pure *rajas* born of the mark of that body, it emerged from the fiery energy (*tejas*).
The Lord Hari, the creator of dreams, dwells in that subtle throat;
there resides the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that the eleven sense organs must perform their respective functions.
That [intention] arises in the mind, yet one does not carry it out through effort; for sleep, ignorance, madness, fear, disease, exhaustion, and intoxication are obstacles to the wise. (PS 1.8.77)
She remains favorable even in successive future births;
however, for deeds not performed, there is but a dream.
It bestows the fruits of one's own lord.
The infinite objects seen in a dream bestow pleasure and pain at that very time;
they do not follow the path of waking vision, but are merely imagined at that moment. (PS 1.8.79)
The Lord, having taken as his material cause the infinite latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the healthy living being during sleep,
[manifests] the Taijasa state by means of those very same primary factors mentioned previously.
Having fashioned numerous objects, the Lord of All manifests them;
therefore, a dream is real because it indicates future results.
Moving in that manner during the appropriate time for all other living beings, such as Śeṣa and others,
one becomes a creator of dreams for people, being both composed of fire (taijasa) and a dream-maker.
Taking hold of that quality of tamas, the wise one, remaining subtle within the heart,
[perceives] the world-teacher who resides at the feet of the individual soul bound by the subtle body.
In this way, with one face, he bestows the state of meditative absorption (dhyāna) from the body;
swallowing half of that which is bound by the subtle body (liṅga), he brings about the state of swoon (mūrchā).
Having placed the *liṅgabaddha* at the mouth, the wise one, by means of a very slight transformation of form,
when the God embraces him, then bestows sleep.
The wise one is indeed the Lord of the individual soul (jīva); without him, the jīva is considered incapable of action.
Having reached the wise one situated in the throat, he becomes the dreamer of dreams for all living beings.
Having seized the individual soul (jīva), this Lord of the World has awakened within the right eye;
for the two elements of wisdom and radiance do not initiate dreaming or sleep.
Because he avoids those various evil karmas even without being in a state of meditative absorption, they call the wise one the Lord of Life; he is present within the hearts of all.

That wise one, having placed the living being consisting of parts within his own form by means of a single form at his feet, takes up the consciousness along with its subtle [elements] in a formless state, established in his heart.
When that wise son, together with his characteristic marks, shall have become one with the All,
he will become one with the one residing in the heart.
The Lord, the husband of the living beings (Jīva), even brings about the state of meditative absorption;
Viśva and the others bestow the three states upon those who are partless.
Except for the upright ones among all the gods born on earth, the Teacher of the World causes those who follow wisdom to abide in the three states.
Always instigating wakefulness for those dwelling in the higher worlds,
the All-pervading Lord thus created Brahmā by means of the subtle body.
In this way, Saṅkarṣaṇa, having assumed a subtle body through the power of Vāyu and Jayā,
caused Vāsudeva to make Sarasvatī the wife of Brahmā.
Saṅkarṣaṇa, however, made the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) the husband of Bhāratī;
and Pradyumna became the creator of the subtle body for Sarasvatī, that is, Bhāratī.
From those two [elements], their respective subtle bodies (*tanmātra*) became the remaining [subtle elements];
at that time, the wind was named *sūtra*, and Brahmā was named *puruṣa*.
For even in the creation of all eternal things, such as the Vedas and so forth, as well as the continuum of individual souls—
which are themselves eternal— those two [the intellect and the ego] possess the conceit of being their creators.
Without those two wives, not even the slightest purpose can endure;
for Brahmā, being free from egoism, though possessing a body, is as if bodiless.
By names such as "the bodiless wind," "cloud," and "lightning," all those who possess the conceit [of being knowers] should express the three supreme whitenesses through their yoga. (PS 1.8.99)
Then, in due course, Aniruddha became the creator of the subtle body for Brahmā, Vāyu, and their wives, twenty-one, twenty-four, and twenty-one times respectively.
Recited twenty-one times three over, the subtle [Aniruddha] bestows a body;
Aniruddha likewise [bestows a body] for those afflicted by grief and for those who are blue-complexioned and so forth.
And [he knows] the three beginning with Sauparṇī, according to the sequence of time and place,
as well as all the tattvas without exception, from Indra down to Puṣkara.
Aniruddha, however, performed [the meditation] twenty-one times;
and whenever one attains subtlety, it occurs at that very preceding moment.
Furthermore, there is a disparity in the subtle bodies (*liṅga*) of those various groups of living beings,
due to their being drawn out in every respect for five or seven months.
From Hari, however, there arose the subtle creation of the real deities;
thereafter, he [the unmanifest] was joined with a state of imbalance between sattva and tamas.
The Creator of the universe thoroughly set in motion the primordial nature (prakṛti) known as Jaḍā;
from that, the triad of bindus arose: sattva, rajas, and tamas.
In the upper region is the sattva-bindu; below that is the rajas-bindu; and below that is the tamas-bindu. These three initial bindus are gross. (PS 1.8.107)
She who assumes the forms of Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā, and who presides over the three qualities (guṇas) in sequence, is [the Goddess];
while Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva are the regulators of the sequence of the Bindu.
Brahmā and Vāyu, together with their two wives, are the two possessors of the three forms;
indeed, Śrī rests upon the impermanent drops of sattva and the other qualities.
When there is an imbalance in the drops (*bindu*) of *rajas* and *tamas*, the Lord of the World, Brahmā, and Saṅkarṣaṇa, having extracted [the world], protected it. (PS 1.8.110)
Then the unborn Viṣṇu, residing within the drop of sattva, causes it to increase;
he then created there the first veil of sattva, which was occupied with its task.
The one named Brahman is situated within a speck of dust; in the region below that is the second enclosure, which belongs to the one named Rājasa.
Rudra, situated within the *tamobindu*, fashioned the *tāmasa* enclosure;
for that is indeed the second enclosure, contained within the womb of *rajas*.
Indeed, in the third enclosures are Viṣṇu and Brahmā, Śiva and Vāyu—each pair accompanied by their consorts—and Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā, who are to be worshipped first. (PS 1.8.114)
The two [beings] take pride in the three qualities (guṇas) of the gross body residing within their respective selves:
the first is white, the second is red, and the third is blue. (PS 1.8.115)
Due to the imbalance of the quality of rajas within the enclosure of the three qualities,
that king named Brahmā established the enclosure of Mahat.
The fourth enclosure therein consists of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva;
from the two born of Brahmā and Vāyu, two triple-formed [beings] were produced.
Brahmā and Vāyu, together with their wives, are the presiding deities of the principle of Mahat;
the Lord who governs the principle of Mahat is Hari himself, known as Ānanda.
The two sons of Ānanda were Brahmā and Vāyu, who had attained greatness;
due to the imbalance of the quality of rajas, they are considered to possess all the constituent parts (kalās) in their entirety.
Likewise, from the rajasic portion of the ten sense organs, the kalās arise;
and from the tamasic portion, the tanmātras arise as the five kalās pertaining to the Mahat.

The sixteen digits (kalās), though eternal, are non-existent [independently]; they are perpetually present as the transformations of the Great Principle (mahattattva) arising from the gross body of Brahmā.
From [the principle] subject to Ānanda, the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) is born; it is considered to be of three types:
Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa. Thus, the "I" is threefold. (PS 1.8.122)
Because it possesses the radiance of the rising sun, I am called the Great Three-Colored One;
however, that which is born from the portion of *sattva* is the transformative (*vaikārika*), and is declared to be white.
The Taijasa [body], arising from the portion of Rajas, is proclaimed to be red in color;
it consists of the mind, the senses, and the subtle elements in their prior subtle form.
For these [energies] residing in the Great Principle (mahattattva) are sequentially supported by the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra):
Brahmā is the presiding deity of the Gāyatrī-vidhi in the quality of goodness (sattva), while Viriñca resides in the quality of passion (rajas).
He truly becomes Sāvitrīśa in darkness, named Brahman;
he dwells as Sarasvatīśa when those three forms have arisen.
Brahmā and Vāyu, who possess these three forms and bear those names, reside in the Great Principle (mahat);
they are present in those three [vows], Gāyatrī and the others, by means of the three beginning with Knowledge (vidyā).
In due order, by the will of Hari, Brahmā, Vāyu, and Śeṣa became his seats;
and Vipaścit and Śeṣa, together with their wives, were the three pillars of dust in the great assembly hall.

By Hari’s command alone, Rudra, who possesses three forms, presides over the three kinds of egoistic principles (*ahaṃkāra*) arising from *vidyā* and the other [tattvas], beginning with *brahman*. (PS 1.8.129)
Accompanied by his wife and characterized by the threefold ego, he possesses a gross body;
this is considered the "Great Enclosure" (mahadāvaraṇa) situated within the Great Principle (mahattattva).
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā-Vāyu, accompanied by their wives,
are always present within all the principles already mentioned and those yet to be described.
Without them, the remaining lords, beginning with Viṣṇu, are nowhere capable of acting;
for the Teacher of the World creates the principle of mind (manas-tattva) from the Vaikārika [ego].

Having created [the ego], that bull among men placed it within the womb of the *ahaṃkāra*; and from the *taijasa* (fiery) *ahaṃkāra*, as it underwent transformation, Hari brought forth the sense organs.
The five powers of knowledge and the five powers of action were created;
however, at the time of creation, the five elements to be created were indeed yet to come into being.
Wherever the Lord was to be established, there he sequentially created those [elements];
from the transformation of space, however, the mere quality of touch arose from Hari.
Then, having produced wind, he spread out the covering of wind;
and from the transformation of that very wind, the mere form [of matter] then came into being.
Then, having produced fire, Hari spread a veil of fire;
yet from that very fire, as it underwent transformation, he created nothing but water.
Then, having produced water, he formed the veil of water;
and from the Lord as he was undergoing transformation within that watery covering, the subtle element of smell (gandha-mātrā) arose.
Then Hari, having fashioned the earth, created the encircling boundary of the world.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā. The Blessed Lord said:
"Within the covering of the earth, that which is suitable for the production of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) [is situated]."
It is measured at fifty million yojanas.
The Blessed One, who knows place and time, left a portion of the teaching unexpounded;
likewise, he did not explain the unconditioned principles (asaṃskṛtadharmas) and those situated above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
That entire [universe] merged within it is proclaimed as the Egg (aṇḍa).
Viṣṇu, named Vijñāna, is the protector of the ego (ahaṅkāra). // PS_1,9.3 //
In the subtle elements of the senses, the Lord of Ramā bears their respective names;
as space, air, and fire, the Lord of all bears the name Prāṇa.
That which is called "Anna" on earth is also concealed by the covering of water;
it is the specific earth that takes the form of a double-layered enclosure around the cosmic egg.
Water, fire, air, ego, and the great principle—these are the qualities;
the coverings of the earth, beginning with sattva and the others, are situated above the egg in successive order.
The tenfold increases are to be understood: passion (rajas) is twice the amount of darkness (tamas);
goodness (sattva) is twice the amount of passion; therefore, there is nothing anywhere that is merely composed of primordial matter (prākṛta).
But in the region above and behind, Hari is of the nature of Aniruddha;
his body is even greater than that [of Pradyumna], and he too has the form of an enclosure.
Beyond those are two [energies] named Pradyumna and Saṅkarṣaṇa;
Vāsudeva stands above them and is considered to be ten times greater than their combined measure.
Even beyond that, in the infinitely infinite-fold space consisting of infinite-infinite pradeśas, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are all-pervading; for them, there is no boundary anywhere.
The glory of the teaching is infinite in space and time, for its qualities are indeed endless nowhere else;
it was first made manifest by the upright ones through direct perception from the Unobstructed One.
Together with the previously mentioned time, the two—Brahmā and Vāyu—were born accompanied by their wives; they possess three forms and proceed respectively through the cycles of the three qualities.
The functions of those [elements], beginning with existence (satva), are proclaimed as the gross bodies;
from that [state] where the subtle body has been restrained, the two—creation and maintenance—are brought about.
Those two, Ṛju and Kau, are considered to have reached the Great Principle (mahattattva) four times;
for they indeed declare that the Great Principle itself is their gross body.
Then those two, Śāntīśa and his consort, became upright and took on female forms respectively;
both of them, having entered into the threefold ego-consciousness, became husbands and wives.
In twenty-one births, those who have directly perceived the principles beginning with the mind-principle (manas-tattva) and others are born outside the cosmic egg, numbering one hundred upright ones.
Thus, the lords of the principles (tattveśas), beginning with Rudra, are each appropriate to their own specific number and rule;
they are capable of creation outside the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) as overseers of perception, but none others ever [possess this capacity].
Thus, having arisen from the three forms previously through the Lord of Peace (Śāntīśa) by way of time,
immediately after the birth of the subtle one, the remaining three [arise] beginning with Ṛju.
The six beginning with Nīla arise from the conjunction with Time; those beginning with Sāparṇī arise in sequence from Aja, Īśa, Ajerā, and Aśeṣya, each by three [factors] beginning with Ajerā.

Those possessing gross bodies, whose nature consists of the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva), were composed of forms; however, others were those who had directly realized the state worthy of that [subtle] level.
In that very same way, within the twenty-one principles beginning with Mahat-tattva, they exist in those respective forms;
for they have not been previously obstructed in their arising from the subtle principles.
The principles beginning with *manas* assumed gross bodies;
those from Indra down to Puṣkara were born from the subtle principles and from Aniruddha.
Through twenty-one gates, they were established in the principles beginning with consciousness (*citta*);
those principles, beginning with the gross (*sthūla*), indeed became their bodies in due order. (PS 1.9.23)

First, those beginning with Indra arise from Śāntīśa; possessing mind and a gross body, they are born two, three, five, or six times, having reached the senses of hearing and so forth, as well as the skin.
Those born on the seventh, sixth, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth lunar days are, respectively, Indra and the others, ending with Puṣkara; they possess gross bodies beginning with speech.

Then, from the fivefold arising [of the elements], through the conjunction of time and by the power of Śāntīśa, the gross bodies consisting of sound and the other [objects] were produced; thereafter, those moving in pairs [the senses] arose.
In this regard, it is held that the state of those deities already mentioned, as well as of those yet to be and those established in their positions, depends upon the nature of their gross bodies.
Aniruddha, the subtle agent who knows the true nature of place, time, and purpose, having first reached their appropriate location, performed the creation.
But for those who abide in all principles and are upright, the subtle-bodied sentient atoms,
increasing tenfold at each stage, proceed everywhere.
Atoms of rajas and tamas attain elevation by the measure of a foot,
having entered the subtle bodies of Rudra, Indra, and others born many times over.
Likewise, atoms of living beings, as well as those of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, are accumulated; these subtle particles reside within the deities such as Rudra and Śakra.
By means of two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven,
and twelve years, they will indeed increase in succession by one-tenth.
For that very reason, by means of the aforementioned preceding causes,
dullness of intellect and other such defects are held to exist in each subsequent form.
And in the principles beginning with Mahat, above the cosmic egg, states such as possession by Daityas are not admitted,
just as rajas and tamas have increased within the subtle bodies.
Thus it has been declared by you that even within the gross bodies,
the atoms of rajas and tamas will indeed manifest in due course.
The principles (tattvas) are its prior forms, and they are infinite;
yet among all the principles, they are straightforward, having manifested both the higher and the lower.
Together with their wives, they abide within all principles, whether low or high;
through the excessive accumulation of the atoms of *rajas* and *tamas*, there arises a perversion of the intellect.
None of them shall ever depart, for they are eternally dear to Hari;
indeed, Brahmā, Sarasvatī, and Viṣṇu arise from all his limbs.
From the left channel arise Śeṣa and Viṣṇu, as well as Śiva;
Nīla and others, Āvāruṇī, the eastern [directions], Indra, and Kāma, who is the mind-born.
The teacher of the Buddha, Manu, was present there along with his wife;
Dakṣa emerged from [Brahmā’s] thumb, as did the sons of Kāma and the Manus who were preceded by Kāma.
From his breath arose the Maruts; from his eye, the Sun; from his hearing, the Moon;
from his heart, Dharma together with his wife; and from his tongue, Varuṇa.
Bhṛgu was born from his skin, Agni from his mouth, Manu from his generative organ, and Viśvāmitra, Marīci, and the others from his urine and excrement. // PS_1.9.42 //
From the aggregate (skandha) came Bhava and Gaṇapati; from the navel and the feet came Śambhu and Jayanta; from the two nostrils came the two Nāsatyas; and from the mouth arose Viṣvaksena.
From the feet arise the Ṛtus (or Ṛbhus),
and from the throat arise the gods born of action (Karmadevas).
The Rudras [emerged] from the cheeks and the Vasus from the forehead of the Lord at his will.
The Ādityas arise from the light and are situated in the row of teeth;
Sanaka and the others, born of the mind, are on the sides near the navel, along with Jayā and the others.
The Gaṅgā and other rivers [issue] from the channels of the Lord through his big toes and so forth;
all those not explicitly mentioned are considered by the wise to have arisen from his side-glance.
Śani [is born] from the body; Puṣkarā and the others arise from the organs of action (karmendriya).
Their wives, whose deities have not been mentioned, were born together with their husbands.
For these [deities], established in the principles (tattva) of Hari and Īra across all principles without exception,
dwell as presiding deities (abhimānin), having arisen sequentially from the limbs [of the mantra] as they have been proclaimed.
Thus, during creation, he is outside the cosmic eggs, and thus, during liberation, he is under the control of Hari;
for in every birth, whatever desire arises, his son is that very destiny.
Caṇḍa, Jayā, and the others stationed at the gates; likewise Śaśāṅka, Dhanada, and all the lords of the Gandharvas, who are also truly present within the various classes of beings.
Those not mentioned are proclaimed to have their exaltations in Puṣkara and Budha;
thus, for all the remaining [planets], they arise from the external egg through their respective divisions.
For there are nine crores of gods who conceive pride in the reality of sentient beings;
from the Unborn (Aja) comes Vipas, and from Nīla comes Viṣaṭkavipavallabhā.
From him [the Self] came Indra; from him, the Moon; from that, all the Maruts beginning with Prāṇa;
from Indra came Dakṣa; and from him, the divine sages such as Nārada and others.
From Indra came Guru, from him Sūrya, and from him Vighnaprabhu was born;
it is remembered that Agni arose from Sūrya, and from Agni the Rudrakas.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Viśvedevas, Aśvins, the Lord of the Rakṣasas,
Parjanya, Budha, Śani, and the others, ending with Puṣkara, have arisen.
The Garuḍas dwell among all principles, as do the deities of the path;
the teachers of the highest ones are themselves lowly, yet they are servants of the highest.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"Indeed, the rays of Viṣṇu and Vāyu are straight throughout."
Whether situated inside or outside of an egg, they obtain birth through various means.
To delude the Asuras, all those beginning with Rudra—who have realized Brahman directly and whose nature is truly meditated upon—appear as if born of another [source]. (PS 1.10.2)
Indeed, those born from the wind [the vital breath] become possessed by the lords of egoism;
for the creation of all the lowly occurs through the limbs or parts of the body by means of the highest [principles].
Thus, emanation has been described in its sequential order; dissolution is traditionally held to occur in the reverse order.
Here, the lords of the principles (tattvas) situated above the cosmic egg are [to be understood] according to the method previously stated.
Indeed, at the time of creation, whatever various things arise in whatever manner, they are well-initiated and free from connection with defects.
After the creation of the qualities (guṇas), all beings were born with gross bodies;
they possessed portions [of the divine], bliss, power, knowledge, and direct perception of space and time.
Absorption in the states of dissolution and emanation, and the splendors characterized by the [three] qualities—
thus are proclaimed the fourteen great gradations.
In the Vedas, in space and time, in the subtle bodies, in the Imperishable, in primordial nature, in all living beings, in the principle of the Great (mahat), and in the three qualities; PS_1,10.8 //
The portions of the upright ones indeed exist; for there is no portion to be discarded among them.
In egoism, there is a portion to be discarded; therein, the portions of Indra and the other gods do not exist.
O best of gods, those who are very lowly in mind dwell in bodies and such things by means of their portions; however, those who are not lowly indeed enter into their own superiors.
Thus, within and without the cosmic egg, there arises a cognition of gradation based on partiality;
yet through the injunction, there is union with all limbs, even for speech, mind, and word.
The Lord bestows union with the limbs of his own manifestation upon the gods;
for the highest, there is great bliss, while for those who are lowly and base, it is associated with their own condition.
That [bliss] which reaches the highest state is inferior to the bliss of the base by a hundredfold;
clearly, the bliss of those in Śvetadvīpa and other such places who have attained liberation is superior by a hundredfold.
In three locations—the portion of Śrī, the portion of Cinmātrānanda, and the portion of Bhūdurgā—pure bliss is to be attained by those of sattvic nature. (PS 1.10.14)

The Lord [is worshipped] by the continuous line of devotees with hair, with infinite objects fit for enjoyment that are pure and characterized by goodness (sāttvika), and with those things fashioned from earth and water.
That self-ruling Person bestows his own bliss in abundance upon the noble and only in small measure upon the base, according to each one's fitness.
In liberation, there is no desire for even the slightest bit of the excellent enjoyments of one's own superior state; indeed, for one who is full of self-bliss, there is no rebirth.
For one whose linga has been shattered, suffering, ignorance, and so forth are not held to arise again;
for they say that the word "hundred" refers to having reached ten thousand.
The strength of the supreme is vast, while that of the lowly is indeed meager;
yet Śeṣa, remaining within the waters of the womb, supports the entire earth with a single crest.
He always supports the islands, oceans, rivers, and mountains like a mustard seed;
that very Śeṣa has a thousand mouths, and the mighty Vāyukūrma supports him.
At the tip of the tail, those preceded by Śakra (the gods) hold it; the remaining many, such as cows, buffaloes, and others, are inferior in strength compared to the single elephant’s meal.
Even if these were to assemble by the millions— tortoises as well as elephants— they would never be able to fight against the Naga.
Likewise, thousands of millions of low-ranking gods were assembled by the superior gods through their power; how much more so, then, the immortal Rākṣasas?
Therefore, by means of this power, the relative gradation of all beings has been discerned,
without regard for those situated inside or outside the cosmic egg throughout infinite kalpas.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, he always knows the past, present, and future objects and their accumulations, as clearly as an amalaka fruit in the palm of his hand.
Having contemplated for an exceedingly long time those qualities of Nārāyaṇa— which are beginningless, eternal, non-increasing, without distinction, and without interval— he too [attained them].

One is certainly not capable of knowing even a single portion of that one divided infinite part, which itself constitutes an infinite fraction of [the Buddha] who is filled with infinite auspicious qualities.
For the knowledge of the upright person, which knows the qualities of the Lord, is indeed capable of taking the past and future worlds as its object. (PS 1.10.28)

Having observed that the knowledge of the Vaiṣṇavas is indeed superior to that of all other living beings, and that their knowledge of the distinctions between the pure and the impure is superior even to the constant observation of all things; PS_1,10.29.
It would not be capable of making the world, which is divided from those superior to oneself, an object [of knowledge] by means of only one part; for these [beings] do not know otherwise.

Whether they be inert or unconscious, from Śiva down to Puṣkara, those bound by the *liṅga*, those established in the *pada*s, those who are to be, and those who have attained direct realization; PS_1,10.31 //
Whether within the cosmic egg or outside it, those who exist in their true nature in manifold forms do not know the world in its entirety.
The knowledge of all beginningless living beings is considered to be twofold: internal (svārūpika) and external (bāhya). The internal is held to be eternal. (PS 1.33)
The unborn and eternal [Self] of Viṣṇu is always subject to bondage;
through the process of sequential yoga, it comes under the control of the Lord of the individual soul (jīva) and is subject to Māyā.
Manifested by the means of attainment (sādhana) until the end of liberation, thereafter it is a single mode of ignorance, devoid of that which relies on its own superior [cause]. (PS 1.10.35)
The Lotus-born knows the infinite qualities of Viṣṇu as proclaimed in the Vedas, whether they reside in the Lord or in the world, though his knowledge falls short by a hundredfold.
Whether established on a station or liberated, others besides them who abide in those qualities are worshippers of Viṣṇu; they possess knowledge that is progressively less by one hundred than his.
That which is produced repeatedly and clearly within the mind of one who is always straightforward and relies upon both the ordinary and extraordinary bodies; (PS 1.10.38)
Their fivefold cognition consists of both that which has an external mode of operation and that which is always in accordance with reality; however, it occurs only at certain times, not at all times.
Devoid of possession by demons and the like, they are always free from undesirable objects;
even though accompanied by the sense organs, they remain so while these are enveloped by the subtle sense organs within the *liṅga*.

When the cognition produced by the gross sense organs—which are intensely attached to their respective objects—is itself devoid of defects, that cognition born of sound reasoning is indeed valid. (PS 1.10.41)
However, that knowledge which arises from reasoning is said to be inferential;
its means of proof are perception, inference, and scripture. (PS 1.10.42)
Just as it is [valid] in that way from hearing the meaning of the Vedic scriptures,
so too the knowledge born of the mind arising from one's own tradition is indeed knowledge of the object as it truly is.
In due order, they are supported by the principles (tattva) from one region to another;
however, at the time of the activity of the principles, they possess powers appropriate to their own nature.
Knowledge arising from scripture is proclaimed to be threefold;
that which arises from the mind is said to be external action.
Perception and inference, as well as scripture, are the means of establishing that [reality].
The living soul is the knower, the objects are the things to be known, and these are considered the causes.
Furthermore, the cognition of Rudra and others, which arises externally within the mind,
is impermanent even though it is established by the three valid means of knowledge beginning with perception.
In some cases that cognition is in accordance with reality, while in other cases it may be contrary to reality;
[these include] those born of karma, those born of gods, and those born of ignorance, such as divine servants and slaves, who are progressively inferior.
All beings, from the gods and gandharvas down to [the lower realms], are proclaimed to possess parts;
yet those from the eternal immortals and gandharvas down to the grasses are without parts.
The nature of these souls is knowledge that is eternal and corresponds to reality;
it ranges from the most excellent down to the inferior, and so on, in order, including that which does not correspond to reality.
External objects are produced and impermanent, and for the most part always correspond to reality;
whether in the case of God or the world, they possess progressively less depth of penetration.
Thus, there is a great degree of gradation in knowledge among the various high and low gods;
even among those of upright nature, portions of the three great qualities (guṇas) exist in elevated states.
In that region, there are never any portions of deities such as Rudra; however, in the regions below it, there are always portions of deities such as Ahaṅkārarudra.
There, Indra and the other gods do not abide, nor those who dwell in regions lower than that;
for the boundaries of spirits and non-humans are declared to be such as they are in each respective region.
The sixteen digits (kalās) and their respective abodes are then continuously pervaded by those [elements];
the mind, sound, the sense of hearing, and speech have the digits of space as their continuous support.
The categories known as skin, touch, and hand reside in air;
the categories known as eye, form, and foot reside in fire within the body.
The [energies] of the tongue, taste, and the secret organ are supported by the water element;
the [energies] of smell, the nose, and the generative organ are supported by the earth covering.

The portions of the faculties consisting of mind alone [are assigned] to the elements in successive order; by virtue of that authority, Śakra and the others, ending with Puṣkara, were appointed by Hari.
At the time of the arising of the subtle and the gross, those who are superior go to higher regions,
while those who are increasingly inferior remain in high places due to their reliance on gods who are themselves high and low.
But from the [highest] region, they are established in the principles (tattvas) in successive order;
however, at the time of the activity of the principles, they possess powers appropriate to their own essential nature.
Thus they speak of the great gradations appropriate to the regions,
according to the measurement of the gods, for a hundred years, established by the sequence of before and after.
The birth of the *ṛjus* is said to occur at intervals of one thousand years;
likewise, the *vipādins*, Indras, and so forth [arise] at intervals of ten thousand years.
Arising in succession from prior to posterior, occurring as low or high over time;
now, the gradation of direct perceptibility for everything is being analyzed.

When the time for the extraction of the essential nature of all living beings, from grasses upward, has arrived— that is, at the time appropriate for the spiritual practice of each specific being— [the Teacher appears].
And by his command, Hari, Śrī, Brahmā, and Vāyu, together with their wives,
[established] all the inhabitants born in these other continents and regions in every respect.
Wandering through heaven, the atmosphere, and the earth, he beheld living beings subject to their own karma, existing in various wombs and dwelling in the subterranean realms such as Atala.
Desirous of uplifting [the world], the Blessed One will cause those who have arisen from human wombs— and among them, the best of Brahmins— to be born in Bhārata.
There, by means of an action that manifests his vast form in its entirety,
he unites [the disciples] with the supreme gurus who bestow the knowledge appropriate for all.
Hari joins together everything—from grass up to mortals and the Gandharvas—in different places and at different times; for they are indeed infinite in number.
They are partless; they are those who take hold of the symbols; they are practitioners of karma-yoga;
they range from the gods and gandharvas down to those born of their own nature, in their entirety.
Those yogins of knowledge who possess parts and take up non-symbolic supports ascend gradually;
because they perceive that which resides in the symbol and that which resides in the body, they are called by that name.

Because the Lord is seen outside of the subtle body (pratīka), those who take the non-subtle as their support are generally practitioners of yoga whose knowledge is directed toward the deities of ritual action.
For these [beings], birth within an egg and the direct realization [of truth] are praised;
however, at the time of maturity, being partless, they depart [from the body] and go to the worlds beginning with Maharloka.
Upon their dissolution, there is no entry into their own higher [realms];
for those beginning with the gods and gandharvas, dissolution occurs through ascending to a higher plane.
They declare that for the yogi, entry into his own superior [bodies] within the Mahālaya occurs from the subtle body (lūkṣmadeha),
whether by way of upward departure or non-departure, according to the will of Tatpuruṣa and Īśvara.
Those belonging to the *puṣkara* and *tāttvika* classes never undergo departure or dissolution;
indeed, through their gross bodies, they enter into those who are superior to them.
The yogis who practice the yoga of devotion call these the successive stages;
for indeed, virtuous action, knowledge, and devotion are always present for all of them.
All of them are necessarily such due to the predominance of those respective [qualities],
being partless [in their nature] because of thousands of births suitable for the realization of the Truth.

Having attained knowledge through ten [qualities] and true devotion through three, they behold that which resides in the heart and are thereby liberated; thus, they are indeed practitioners of Karma-yoga.
By performing virtuous deeds without desire for reward, they obtain the lineage of the Guru;
those who are not established in reality, being servants of the gods, [attain this] after hundreds of births of virtuous deeds.
Having performed [meritorious deeds] over ten thousand births and having attained knowledge,
and having attained devotion through three hundred [births], the practitioners of knowledge-yoga are liberated.

Therefore, those who are deities of action and, beyond them, the practitioners of the yoga of devotion, perceive Him residing within their own hearts through births appropriate to them, beginning with the state of grass and so forth. (PS 1.10.82)
The power [of the yogin] is such that he perceives the Lord, distinguished by the radiance of a lamp, neither as a god nor as one among mortals,
within his own body for half a ghaṭikā, or even in liberation.
The capacity for the worship of pure consciousness alone does not exist in those who possess superior qualities;
for such [worship] would be indirect for them, and not superior. (PS 1.10.84)
Even when they perceive forms such as those of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa externally at times, they perceive them as being human; this is what is remembered through direct perception.
Those [perceptions] that are direct when the gross [mind] resides in the heart become indirect when it is outside;
likewise, there is the vision of the independent one who appears as the individual soul (jīva) abiding in its own essential nature.
Indeed, for everyone, one's own nature is thus directly perceived;
it remains for a mere three-quarters of a ghaṭikā within the natural heart, which is one's true self.
Worms, insects, and the like perceive Hari by means of the light of a lamp;
perception through the eye of one's own true nature is called "direct" (aparokṣa).
The Vedas, space, syllables, time, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśa) are not objects of knowledge by means of the natural senses;
yet, by their very nature, they are indeed proclaimed to be knowable.
When the fivefold ignorance has been destroyed through devotion and the grace of Hari,
[one perceives] the radiant *liṅga*, like a jewel, residing within the subtle body.
The two eyes of the living being become manifest; he sees by means of his own [light], abiding in the nature consisting of light, which resides sequentially within the gross heart.
Insects and the like are the size of a barley grain; spiders are the size of a jujube fruit;
bulls are the size of a thumb-tip; and [the fire] is like the wick of a lamp. (PS 1.10.92)
Deer perceive Hari, the Lord of Ramā, for a duration of but a single *ghaṭikā*—
as a lamp that is equal [to all], consisting of consciousness and bliss, and whose very nature is consciousness and bliss.
Birds, beasts, and cows [perceive] Hari residing within the heart and pervading all living beings,
endowed with the brilliance of a hundred lamps, for half a ghaṭikā or even half of that.
"O King, men should meditate upon the Lord as the Self, which is Truth-Consciousness-Bliss;
as for lightning, O kings, men should know it to be ten times the measure of lightning. (PS 1.10.95)
O gods, the kings [behold him] as having twice that splendor;
the Gandharvas and Pitṛs behold the Lord as resembling a hundred suns.
The cowherd women were worthy of contact with Kṛṣṇa’s body; those born of the earth shone like five thousand suns, while even those born of fire possessed the luster of ten thousand suns.
Even among the multitude of living beings numbering eighty-four lakhs plus four lakhs,
only ten persons are said to be truly real, and of those, five are [the most] essential.
The five [elements] are considered inferior to Parjanya and superior to Puṣkara;
together with their consorts, yet devoid of Soma, they are situated both within and without the Egg.
There are thirty Cāraṇas and seventy Rākṣasas among all the classes;
however, in the intermediate space, those born from the lotus remain as far as the realm of Brahmā.
Likewise, within each individual day throughout the course of a year,
all [parts] possessing portions are unreal according to the enumeration that will be stated.
In every eon, moreover, there are those established in their stations who perceive directly;
indeed, there are hundreds of Apsarases, such as Urvaśī and others, equal in number to the [digits of the] moon.
Those who are equal to those born of ignorance are limited; others are equal to the gods of merit (*karmadeva*).
A hundred [lives] among the ancestors (*pitṛs*) are equal to seven [lives] among them, and these are equal to [the lives of] Urvaśī and others.
Others are inferior to those born of noble lineage, yet superior to them in successive order;
among them, the Gandharvas are a hundredfold, and eight are equal to those born of karma.
All those twenty supreme sages numbered one hundred crores;
among them, for that long, they remained content with the hundreds of pleasures born of their karma.
The others besides those born of noble lineage are equal even to the sons of Agni;
there are sixteen thousand and thirty hundred of the Cāraṇas and Rākṣasas.
Likewise, there are seventy others who have achieved their goals among all classes;
these hundred known as the Siddhas and Ājānas perceive the soul residing within the heart.
The gods of karma perceive the light of ten million suns, which resides within the heart yet extends outward, equal in extent to the fourteen worlds; they take hold of these as their physical forms.
Mortal men [perceive] for only two ghaṭikās; the best of kings [perceive] up to three nāḍīs;
likewise, human gandharvas [perceive] up to four nāḍīs, O Lord.
The Gandharvas [reside] at the end of six nāḍīs, while the Guhyakas [reside] at the end of the yāma;
and the Ṛṣis, the sons of Agni, reside at the end of ninety-nine koṭis.
The Karmadevas behold the Supreme Lord, the Teacher of the World, for a period of ten ghaṭikās beginning from sunrise until the end of midday.
Those who are free from rivalry with their own superiors, who avoid ill-conceived undertakings,
who are devoid of ignorance in the form of objective existence, and who are free from the possession of demonic influences.
At the time of the radiance previously described, those who are real and free from the aforementioned defects always behold that Lord of the World, Hari.
Indeed, these faults are seen in their full extent among the base;
among the highest of the high, they are few, and even those that exist are considered negligible.
No connection with faults is ever seen anywhere in Brahmā;
kings are preceded by mortals, gandharvas, and the sixteen [classes of beings].
The hundreds, the ten thousands, the hundreds of thousands, the millions, the billions, the arbuds, and even all qualities beyond those— [all these belong to Viṣṇu].

One who has attained Brahman meditates upon the infinite qualities declared in the Vedas, and no other; likewise, those born as mortals meditate upon the gods within their hearts, and those established in their stations upon the deities of the sacred seats.
Likewise, they see the gods residing in the coverings, as well as the mandala,
the *suṣumnā*, and the seven lotuses within the Lord of that cave.
The lords of the stations and the lords of the roots are the mortal singers;
they reside in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels, moving upward in sequence throughout the entire body.
Having meditated upon and worshipped all the forms of Hari residing within that [tattva], the gods known as the *ājānajā* are liberated. (PS 1.10.120)

And these, stationed as individual forms and clinging to the feet of Hari, are the *karmadevas*; though they do not possess mastery over the principles (*tattvas*), they assume all manner of forms in every respect.

Even those who worship the form of Virāj are liberated upon having fully worshipped it; however, those who rely on non-symbolic supports, as well as the gods of action and the celestial deities, [attain their respective goals].
For one who has abandoned the marks [of renunciation], for one who is liberated, and even for grass, insects, and so forth—
all these have bodies of their own nature extending for ten yojanas.
From that point, the pain for trees and the like, as well as for deer and the like, becomes double;
and beyond that, for mortals who are liberated, such as Śūdras and others.
The Kṣatriyas, immortals, and Gandharvas always possess a lineage that increases by one, two, three, or four quarters; thereafter, their radiance increases by two, three, or more.
On all sides, from the multitude of gods and gandharvas whose splendor was equal to Mount Meru,
the ancestors were released after a long time, their beauty reaching as far as the Bhuvarloka.
The Gopīs are worthy of contact with Kṛṣṇa’s feet;
their splendors extend through the succession of births, remaining equal from birth until the end of existence, and they illuminate even the realm of heaven.
And for whichever individual soul the light of Hari has been directed toward an object,
by fate that light appears externally to the sight, just as a mortal appears to those standing above.
The body of Being-Consciousness-Bliss cannot be an object of external vision;
having seen and worshipped the Virāṭ-body, the Karma-devas are liberated.
One sees Viṣṇu, who is such a light extending to the end, with the eye that consists of one's own true nature; yet they do not see the Lord at all with the obstructed [eye].
They behold, yet do not worship, the Lord who pervades the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
manifesting in all the forms previously mentioned, from Puṣkara down to Śakra.
Having seen, meditated upon, and worshipped the series beginning with the earth and ending with the principle of mind outside the Egg, all will attain liberation in due course of time.

Those beginning with Puṣkara and ending with Mahendra, who possess progressively greater splendor, are capable of beholding Īśāna as he has entered into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) through his worship. (PS 1.10.133)
Vāmadeva and others worshiped the Lord Hari, the Sovereign whose body pervades the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva), and who possesses the splendor of ten million billion suns.

And having been liberated into the Great Principle (mahattattva), they shall behold Hari, who is spread even within darkness; like those preceded by Aruṇī, they will lead him, who resides in darkness, into the light.
The inexhaustible world, bounded by the horizon, is pervaded by the infinite radiance of the Sun;
yet even after worshipping Him, one attains liberation through speech, and thereafter, a radiance even greater than that [of the Sun] arises.
Brahmā alone perceives that which resides within the enclosure of Vāsudeva, and no one else;
for as long as they perceive him as a living soul (jīva), he indeed appears to them as possessing only common attributes.
As long as Viṣṇu is indeed to be worshipped, so long does he possess a specific manifestation for them;
for he is not merely the common light of Brahmā, but is the lord of specific manifestations.
The portion of the nature of extremely slight happiness residing in living beings is such that it pervades all places, just like the pervasive illusory power (māyā) of the Lord.
Just as the light of a lamp does not shine in the presence of the sun's radiance,
so too the light of those named A-prabha does not shine in the presence of Viṣṇu’s radiance.
In this way, the lower radiance dissolves into the higher radiance;
nevertheless, those who know things as they truly are are liberated and have attained the highest knowledge of reality.
Whoever perceives whatever degree of splendor exists in Hari possesses but a hundredth part of it;
for the highest of the wise know that there is indeed a gradation in luminosity.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"Among men, [the foremost are] Brahmā and Vāyu; among those with feet, the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu)."
Hari always possesses the entry into specific forms and so forth through his male form.
The speech of the Vācīr goddess acts among women in her own form;
Viṣṇu causes the specific possession [of power] according to the fitness of the individual. (PS 1.11.2)
But one among the highest [sages] was possessed by those very gods (his own);
that lord of ascetics performed a most great deed that was impossible for living beings to achieve.
The degree of penetration that is desired in the highest of living beings is not the same in lower beings; therefore, they possess little power.
In this way, among the gods who abide in their stations, there is no penetration leading to liberation;
nor is there penetration into those who are partless, nor even into those born of the womb who possess parts.

For in all manifestations of the vital air (vāyu), there is indeed a specific penetration (viśeṣāveśa) at all times—whether in its essential nature, its subtle signs, its subtle forms, or in gross bodies. (PS 1.11.6)
For the sake of protection, the Lord always dwells within all principles (*tattva*);
yet such an entry (*āveśa*)—known as "special" (*viśeṣa*)—does not exist even among the gods in the case of Viṣṇu.
In some cases manifestation [is taught], in others the rāsa; even among the seven eggs of Brahmā,
it is held that [the soul] exists within the eggs, above the egg, and within the straight paths beginning with the principle of Sadāśiva.
In some cases, the entry of supreme deities into inferior beings is observed; the Lord, for the sake of power, effects his entry even into the asuras.
By him, the arrogant [Asuras] were destroyed by the gods through the will of Hari;
for Viṣṇu remains eternally hidden among the gods.
Knowledge, bliss, power, and other such qualities are considered common [to all];
from grass up to Brahman, even Māyā exists in Hari as well.
Nevertheless, among those who are very base, there are those who rely on the lamp of virtue;
they are common to their own kind, while those of a different kind are distinct.

In the Teacher of the World, there is absolute independence, self-delight, pervasion by excellent qualities, as well as freedom from dependence on others and the like, and the state of being the sovereign controller.
Attributes such as being the creator of the world and so forth are considered to be of a different genus in Hari;
whereas qualities such as imperishability and so forth do not clearly exist in Māyā, but only in Brahman.
Rectitude, natural loftiness, pride in eternal objects, sovereignty over all, and mastery over the effects within the subtle body (liṅgadeha). (PS 1.11.15)
These are known as being of a different class, preceded by the fitness for desirelessness;
these are said to belong to Hari and Īra, but certainly not to Viśeṣa and Śeṣa.
Thus, among these supreme [beings], those of a different kind do not descend to lower states;
however, because of their truth and infinity, their liberation cannot indeed be described.
Starting from the gods of action (karmadevas) up to Brahmā among those embodied beings,
there appear lines such as the discus and conch, as well as arrows, spears, hooks, and so forth.
The javelin, the spear, the transverse ploughshare, the halāhala poison, and the like;
Govinda, the tila seed, wheat, the umbrella, the chowrie, and the archway.
Those with the form of a raised banner or a fan,
those mounted on swings, those resembling fish, tortoises, lions, and so forth, as well as those bearing the bull, the jewel, and other such symbols.
Lines resembling the faces of Garuḍa and Śeṣa reside on the right foot of men and indeed on the left foot of women.
Lines in the shape of a cow, a conch, or a mace on the left side are considered auspicious for men;
they are deficient in form among those of low status, while they possess an exalted form among those of high status.
All the lines are complete within the vital breath (prāṇa), within Māyā, and also within Hara;
therein too, the high-order (uccakra) exists, and the lines are the causes of height.

He who is ninety-six finger-breadths in height, whose proportions are like those of a banyan tree, who is seven paces tall and four cubits in span, and who is endowed with the thirty-two marks; // PS_1,11.24 //
Among the limbs of the body of the virtuous, there is length in five places,
shortness in five, and redness in seven places.
He whose six elevations are perfectly broad,
and whose three qualities possess both depth and lightness, truly shines in these three respects.
He is endowed with excellent marks, and he is indeed the guru who bestows knowledge;
for among the best of mortals, there are indeed twenty characteristics.
Gradually, each one increasing in turn, all the characteristics of the two became fully perfected and endowed with their defining marks.
In the body, in its own nature, and in all the means for the welfare of beings,
these [faculties] are fully manifest in the higher [beings], while they remain unmanifest in others.
Now, hear the gradation in creation—first in the beginning and then in what follows.
The creations of the self, the subtle, the qualities, and the gross have been described previously. (PS 1.11.30)
From the fivefold modification of the unmanifested elements,
there subsequently arose the fivefold ignorance in the form of existence previously described.
The delusion of beings with material bodies occurs even in some cases among those born from manifest sources;
this creation above the egg is proclaimed as the "creation of taste" (rasa-sarga).
The creation beginning with Mahat and ending with the Egg is so designated;
that Egg and all that is within it are proclaimed as the "entirety" (samasta).
People call "anusarga" that which has arisen within the egg;
all the gods, beginning with Mahat, are powerless in the creation of the egg.
Then Hari praised the Puruṣa, who consists of thirty-seven arrows, as well as Time and the entire collection of principles along with their destroyers.
The Unborn One, having taken up and joined together [the elements] through their fortunes, makes them into a single unity;
and the Lord, dividing that into three parts, takes the first portion for Himself.
Having taken up that [seed] named Viṣṇu and swallowed it himself, the Lord of Śrī,
the Sovereign of Puruṣas, deposited his own virility within her.
Within the revolution of the earth, the Teacher of the World, having created the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) with a width of fifty koṭis, brought forth the body of Brahmā. PS_1.11.38 //
Accompanied by all the mind-made caityas, he entered the maṇḍala of the heroes;
within the cosmic egg filled with water, he became the refuge of all worlds.
That Lord Hari, Viṣṇu, known as Padmanābha, was present in the auspicious waters of the cosmic egg (bhūdaṇḍa) within his own primordial nature, being entirely non-different from it.
Endowed with all ornaments, possessing a thousand feet, eyes, and arms, his head turned eastward (or westward), facing upward, he lay down, clothed in yellow garments, poised in equanimity.
At the very beginning of the creation of the cosmic egg, from the triply divided collection of principles,
there arose another egg, which the all-pervading Lord Padmanābha entered.
Having placed that golden gift of earth which he had created upon his navel, he generated a lotus; from its stalk, the earth then came into being.
Containing the seven continents, oceans, and so forth, together with the waters of the mass of darkness,
it extends fifty koṭis [of yojanas] and occupies the central region within the cosmic egg.
Its foundation is extremely firm and vast, measuring one hundred thousand *yojanas*;
below the watery interior, it extends for twenty-five crores less one hundred thousand.

Situated above those [waters] for many yojanas was the earth of Hari; it was called Bhū because it went upon the waters (bhū-ga), and it was named after Viṣṇu, who is the essence of all that exists within the womb of the earth.
Regarding those things yet to be described and those already mentioned—both the insentient and the sentient—their designations are:
the substratum, the protector, the one named "All," the sustainer of all, and the Lord (Īśvara).
Situated in the center of that [ocean] is Mount Meru, square in shape and made of gold;
it measures one hundred thousand yojanas in height and is crowned with peaks of jewels.
Now, it is said that [Mount Meru] is sixteen thousand yojanas in height; with an equal extent, it is a single vast measure, the abode of all the gods.
Above that, rising from the earth by eighty-four thousand yojanas in height and twice that in extent, it is auspicious on all sides.
In the eight directions starting from the east of Meru, there are indeed the abodes of the world-protectors (lokapālas),
all of which are entirely auspicious, measuring one thousand five hundred [yojanas] each.
In the center of that [space], there are four square seats for the Brahmans and the assembly members, four times as wide [as the central area], made of jewels and gold.
Among them were Indra, Agni, Yama the flesh-eater, Varuṇa, Anila, and Śiva,
together with their wives, their limbs, and their retinues.
In its center was a pavilion, and there likewise were those who carry out the commands of that Creator;
therein was Vāṇīśvara, whose head was the excellent hood of the serpent Ananta.
In the midst of the assembly of the world-protectors, in the four directions beginning with the Vindhya,
there are the Samanā and Sarvatobhadra [deities], numbering eight thousand five hundred Tārās.
There are divine trees such as the mandāra and pārijāta, bearing celestial flowers and fruits; there are also rivers and lakes abounding with lotuses and other blossoms.
They were attended by various women and possessed birds such as swans,
while being served by attendants of equal birth who were of the same *ājāneya* breed.
Having served the radiant Udravara, he became one whose range of vision was divine;
his celestial abode was adorned with divine ornaments, garments, and the like.
In its eight directions, beginning with the east, are Mandara, Merumandara, Supārśva, and Kumuda— these being the supporting mountains in order.
Those Yāma palaces are three thousand [yojanas] wide and ten thousand high;
within them grow trees such as the mango, jambu, kadamba, and nyagrodha.
They are eleven hundred *uccas* in height, endowed with fruits resembling elephants;
they shine like gold and jewels, covered by hundreds of branches.
There, flocks of various birds with fragrant flowers upon their wings [perch] above them on the grounds of golden and jeweled mandāra trees.
Nandana, Caitrarathaka, and Vaibhrājaka are thus described; these forests are beyond description, as is the one known as Sarvatobhadra.

In those [mountains], indeed, the Siddhas who fulfill their desires roam about accompanied by women; for those wandering there, there is supreme happiness, free from fatigue and other such afflictions.
From these [trees], with their fallen, shattered fruits possessing bright and excellent sap,
four rivers were produced from the flowing juice at each of the four [sides].
To the north of Meru are mountains two hundred thousand leagues in circumference and extent; they are old, foul-smelling, and unbearable, and are blue, white, and peaked.
The surface of the earth, nine thousand yojanas in extent,
is bounded on all sides by mountains that extend as far as the western ocean.
To the south are Uśīra, Aṣṭādaśasāhasra, Pṛthula, Dvisāhasraka,
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat.
The boundary mountains are said to be equal in width, height, and length to the previously mentioned lands, starting with Nīla and the others, respectively.
To the east of Mount Meru is the Gandhamādana mountain, frequented by various hosts of siddhas and filled with all kinds of jewels.
In the western direction from Meru is the mountain named Mālyavat;
there are two mountains, Ānīla and Niṣadha, which extend [eastward] and are worshipped by the gods.
Those two, previously described, are situated in the sky and adorned with all kinds of excellent trees;
they are located nine thousand yojanas from Meru in each of the four directions.
They say that the vast surface of the earth consists of the regions covered by the Cīna cloth,
as well as the three [regions] beginning with Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya, and Kuru-varṣa.
The golden lands are divided by mountains such as Varṣanīla;
to the east of Gandhamādana lies the land of Bhadrāśva.
To the west of Mālyavat, the region Ketumāla is proclaimed; then follow, in successive order, the regions of Hari, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata.
To the south, the lands divided by the Niṣadha and other mountains are, in order:
Vaivasvata Manu, the mortal devotee, and Ramyakeśvara.
Āryamā is the protector of the ancestors; the worshipper of the tortoise dwells in the golden realm.
Bhūmi is indeed the wife of Ādivarāha, residing in the land of Kuruvarṣa.
Hayāsya’s lay disciple was Bhadraśravas; and in the [next] year were Bhadra and Varṣaka, and two others named Kṛti and Pradyumna, who were honored by Rati and Akāma.
In Ketumālya, he is worshipped by women; indeed, in Bhadraka, he is not present as Jīva;
in Harivarṣa, he is Nārasiṃha, worshipped by Prahlāda.
Rāma, worshipped by Hanumān, is the lord of Kiṃpuruṣa;
to the south of Bhadrāśva lies the region called Bhārata, which is superior in its virtues.
And the younger brother of this Bhārata, who possessed human pride and was a portion of Śeṣa,
was Nārāyaṇa; these two arose from Mūrti and Adharma, the daughters of Dakṣa.
Those two, worshipped by the world, bestow knowledge upon the sage Nārada;
they move to the left and right in Ilāvṛta, to the east of Mount Meru.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are on the eastern side of Meru’s summit;
touching Gandhamādana, they are equal and composed of gold and jewels.
In width and in height, they are each two thousand yojanas;
they are situated within the nine-thousand-fold earth, between the regions of Jaṭhara and Nīla.
The land situated between Devakūṭa and Niṣadha is considered to be of the same extent;
Gandhamādana and Mandara are the two intermediate lands, each six thousand [yojanas] wide.
The land extending horizontally from Meru to the two mountains situated to its east, Gotra and Parigha, is twice that [width]; likewise, Kailāsa and Karavīra are both situated to the south of Meru.
Pavana and Pariyātra are the two mountains situated on the western side of Meru;
likewise, Śṛṅga and Makara are situated to the north of Meru.
The southern and northern ends of Niṣadha are equal to Nīla;
the western ones are created by Mālyavat, extending eastward from Vāmaka.
This entire region, free from impurity, is divided by these [mountains];
in them all, there is an exceedingly beautiful and charming forest abounding in deer.
And among them were women whose forms had never been seen before, facing upward;
the Lord, with his thousand faces, was the remainder of the six non-material elements.
The great Rudra himself, along with Ambā, dwells there in his eightfold form; he constantly worships that supreme Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is the remainder (the residual essence) of that [universe].
Śambhu, whose body is smeared with ashes, is accompanied by Bhavānī; Śaṅkara always resides with his wife in those very eight abodes.
Even she clearly delights her husband through the force of her prārabdha-karma.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā. The Blessed Lord said:
"From the aperture in the shell of the cosmic egg, pierced by the nail of Trivikrama’s foot..."
Then, from the peak of Vaikuṇṭha, water from the outside entered within.
As he was falling, the Creator held him by his lotus feet;
from the water remaining after washing them, he created the celestial river Gaṅgā.
She who is named Aranāmnī and Anāmnī is considered to be the embodied Parighā, who resides separately in the two divisions of Bhū and Durgā and extends through seven syllables.
She is Nandinī in Satyaloka, Nalinī in the realm of asceticism (Tapas),
Mālinī in Janaloka, and Bhoginī in Maharloka.
In the heavenly world she is the Svardhunī; in the abode of Dhruva she is the Viyadgaṅgā;
in the intermediate space she is the Madāpagā; and above Mount Meru, in the realm of Brahmā, she is the Brahmasada.
And as it falls, in sequence toward the four directions starting from the east,
it is called Sītā, Alakā, Kalakanandā, Cakṣus, and the auspicious Bhadrā.
Due to her agitation at the sight of Sītā, she will first be cast down by Hari outside of Ilāvṛta everywhere, and then she will go toward the ocean.
It is said that she, residing in the southern region, was worshipped by Bhagīratha over a long period of time for the sake of purifying the sons of Sagara.
She is called Bhāgīrathī, the sole purifier of all the worlds;
she was drunk up by the royal seer Jahnu and released again by his word.
That Jāhnavī, originating from the region situated at the northern base of Mount Meru,
flows through the seven worlds located below the surface of the earth and to the east.
That very goddess, the triple-pathed river, shines resting upon Nārāyaṇa;
she flows through the three regions beginning with Harivarṣa, located to the east of Ramyaka.
Moving through Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla, the beloved of the ocean flows;
yet in this great region of Bhārata, there are rivers by the thousands.
Śrīraṅga, the one known as Veṅkaṭeśa, Totādri, the place called Puṣkara,
the illustrious Maṣṇa, the Naimiṣa forest, the Gaṇḍakī river, and the site of Badarī.
These eight are self-manifested in Bhārata and bestow all perfections;
there are thousands of lotus-pools beginning with Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
In this Bhārata, humans, ancestors, Siddhas intent on all means of accomplishment, as well as gods and demons, are each devoted to their own respective practices.
In this world, one attains heaven through virtuous action and hell through sinful action;
through false knowledge one reaches darkness, and through true knowledge alone, the abode of Hari.
For in this world, a person attains those deities of reality who abide in their respective stations; some, having become fully manifest on earth, exist as all the incarnations.
All the gods who were established in their positions during the incarnations of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were born upon the earth; they again worshipped the Lord in his original forms.
Even the gods generally become one here with those who are destined for it;
