likewise, even the attendants of the gods, such as Devadāsa and others, are solely intent upon their own respective means of accomplishment.

Indeed, for those residing here, there are injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth, which are both with parts and without parts, and are likewise intent upon their respective means of accomplishment. (PS 1.12.20)
This continent, named Jambūdvīpa, is surrounded by the salt ocean extending for a hundred thousand yojanas; Mount Meru is indeed situated at its center.
Beyond Mount Sumeru lies that auspicious realm, Cailāvṛta, known as Sukumāra; a man who has gone there [is freed] from the curse of Rudra.
Desiring to sport with Pārvatī, he became a woman;
from this [region] the Plakṣa tree is twice as large, surrounded by the oceans of sugarcane juice and wine.
And there are massive mountains there, equal in splendor to Lord Hari;
they extend from the Ocean of Milk as far as the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice.

In the eight regions beginning with Bhārata, there are six other continents as well; the central one was created by Hari for the sake of experiencing the fruits of those meritorious deeds desired therein.
In this world, one is born from sin or indeed from merit alone according to one's desire;
there, however, there is no fixed limit for the lifespan, for life lasts as long as one's merit endures.
There are men and women of beautiful form who bestow wealth suitable for enjoyment;
there are trees that are jewels of merit, and houses that are like grounds of gold.
Indeed, there is no suffering or the like there, even in the absence of untimely death;
for one who has been created by the Lord, all aims are accomplished there by mere wish.
There, the wise worship Hari, whose nature is the sun;
beyond that is the island of Śālmala, which is twice as large and perfectly circular.
Excluding Jambūdvīpa and Puṣkaradvīpa, the ocean of honey, measuring four hundred thousand yojanas, completely surrounds the five middle continents.
In all [continents], there are seven rivers and seven mountains are proclaimed;
these rivers, situated within the seven continents, flow outwards toward the oceans.
All the objects there, crowded with people, are utilized for enjoyment;
the mountains situated there reach as far as the eastern and northern oceans.
Divided by them into seven regions, each depending on its own lineage of Manus,
those dwelling on Śālmala indeed worship Viṣṇu as the inner controller within the moon.

Krauñcadvīpa is twice that size, surrounded by an ocean of two million eight hundred thousand [yojanas] consisting of molten water; it is encircled by the excellent jewel known as sūryakānta and others.
For they indeed worship Viṣṇu, who is contained within Varuṇa;
therefore, Śākadvīpa is twice as large as that and is surrounded by the Ocean of Milk.
In the center of Śākadvīpa, which extends for thirty-two lakhs [of yojanas] and is inhabited by the Upāsakas of the Wind, Hari himself exists in his infinite form.
The Lord has a body fifty thousand yojanas wide and seven hundred thousand yojanas high;
his infinite, radiant faces are turned toward Meru and the Lokāloka mountain.
In that continent, this Sun, the eye of the world, always moves around the perimeter of the wheel-shaped ramparts, situated at a height of one hundred thousand [yojanas].
Circumambulating Mount Meru once every day with the rapid force of its dry wheels, the Maker of Light proceeds.
The northern tip of the Sun’s axle is like an oil-press wheel;
the other [tip], joined with a wheel, is situated on Mount Mānasottara.
They roam within that [ocean] upon the level ground of the earth,
reaching up to a height of forty yojanas from its center.
There are sixty thousand and four very firm pillars, as many as there are connections with the sense organs, and separated by those same intervals. (PS 1.12.42)
One hundred yojanas thick, radiant, made of vajra, and auspicious;
above that, in a pavilion illuminated by jewels a hundred thousand feet high.
With a brilliantly shining mandala extending for ten thousand yojanas, he blazes with the splendor of the sun;
he is the maker of day, the bestower of the fruits of all virtuous means, and the restrainer of Yama.
Situated to the east of Meru, it brings about the rising of those in Bhārata;
to the south of Meru is the middle of the cow-pen (Gomadhya),
where the sun-maker has seven conjunctions.
For those situated in Bhārata, the sun’s position to the west of Meru causes sunset,
while its position to the north of Meru causes midnight for the people of Bhārata.
In the same way, for the people situated in the four directions,
it initiates the morning, midday, midnight, and the half-watch of the night.
Nārāyaṇa himself, his own state of being nourished by the special descent of power (viśeṣāveśa),
[manifests] as one alone through various distinct names by the will of Śrī Hari.
He who is the sovereign lord of the seven islands,
the supreme hand-guarding the suns as they revolve to the right at a height of three hundred thousand [yojanas].
In a dry wheel fashioned from long sticks, extending fifty-six million leagues across and upwards, [beings are cast].
Extending for a hundred yojanas, they shine brilliantly upon the tips of the [stellar] needles;
the nine planets dwell there, following those paths and moving along them.
Those counting-sticks (śalākā) consist of one hundred and eight pieces made of diamond;
they are provided with holes and loops, and are dependent upon the fixed [notch] and the Varuṇa [notch].
By means of each individual part, the supports for the rays are fashioned;
all those sticks are joined with four consciousnesses, and among them, the waters belong to Varuṇa.
And the nooses, having entered within, are situated at a distance of one hundred thousand *lakṣas* from the earth;
likewise, the ends of the axle are positioned in front of the chariot of the Sun.
They are provided with the ends of ropes tied to the tips of the poles and the tips of the axle;
the ropes of the *dhruva* [pole] are likewise joined by the quarters of the constellations in a counter-clockwise direction.
Dhruva causes him, who revolves once every year, to turn rapidly;
his seven horses are of a golden-yellow color and possess great speed.
Equal to those described by the knowers of reality, the elder brother of Garuḍa has them as his reins;
he, Anūru, being swift, yokes them sufficiently with the snares of serpents.
On the summit of Mount Meru, situated at the center of the [world] with its six eyes, in a supreme pavilion fashioned from diamond and adorned with celestial palaces; PS_1,12.58.
The support for the movement of this sun, situated within the vegetable-oil (śāka) ocean,
is Hari, measuring seventy-seven and a half lakṣas from Meru.
Beyond that, on the Mānasottara mountain,
there is a powerful wheel sixty thousand yojanas high.
The wheel made of diamond, possessing a central hole, revolves by the power of Viṣṇu;
it has twelve spokes, six rims, and three channels located within and without.
On the lines of the three axles and the pole of the wheel are the lunar days, the weekdays, and the lords of the planets;
on the others reside the months, and the seasons are situated upon its rim.
The four-month periods are situated on the three naves; the two-year period is in the two outer rims and the axle-hole;
the year is situated on all the wheels, while for the chariot there is but one wheel.
Moving through Cancer and the subsequent signs, the Sun causes the loss of one day [every three days],
while increasing the length of six nights, thereby effecting the southern solstice.
Moving through the six signs beginning with Capricorn, it causes the end of the night; moving through the others one by one, it causes the increase of the days and effects the northern course.
Fifty *vināḍikās* should be added month by month;
elsewhere, the days increase further, and likewise the nights are diminished by half.
But when this [sun] moves through Aries and Libra, day and night are equal;
and in the five signs beginning with Taurus and Scorpio, it creates half-nights.
Moving through the five asterisms beginning with Vṛṣa during the daytime, it produces prosperity;
when the tip of the needle of stars is twenty-eight units high above the three lakṣas.
The constellations beginning with Kṛttikā are situated starting from the northeast and southeast corners;
they are constructed by seven transverse and seven vertical lines.
The stellar sphere is fashioned above the earth at a distance of three hundred thousand [yojanas], by means of lines drawn from each of the two corners.
In each individual tally-stick there are separate perforations;
those four are the forests beginning with Daṃṣṭrākṣa and the rest.
The nine [signs] beginning with Aries, Taurus, Gemini,
Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius.
The bow, the lunar mansion, and the conch, as well as those marked with fish—these nine;
and having entered into each of these, there are one hundred and eight [verses] beginning with the feet.
With the feet [of the asterisms] Dhruva and Sūrya, however, there will be an increase in sequence through all the quarters of the asterisms by means of a counter-clockwise movement.
For twenty ghaṭikās each, over three days, the Moon is bound by Dhruva and Antarhari, respectively, in each quarter of the lunar mansions in due order.
The sun, moving through one constellation in thirteen and a half days,
traverses nine quarters in each of the twelve zodiac signs within a month.
For the sun moves counter-clockwise throughout the year;
the signs beginning with Aries are known as the cavities marked by Aries and the others.
The sun stands at the tip of the pole of the Pole Star (dhruvapāda) in a region elevated by one hundred thousand [yojanas];
the moon stands at the tip of the pole of the Pole Star in a region elevated by two hundred thousand [yojanas].
The moon and the sun are considered to be situated at the locations corresponding to their positions within the circle of asterisms;
the five [planets] beginning with Mars, however, exist above the circle of asterisms.
Constantly bound by the fixed bonds (dhruvapāśa),
the wise one (Jupiter) moves counter-clockwise at a height of five hundred thousand [yojanas], while Mars is at a height of seven hundred thousand.
The sphere of Venus is elevated by nine hundred thousand [yojanas], that of Jupiter by eleven hundred thousand,
while the orb of the Sun is proclaimed to be thirteen hundred thousand.
Indeed, the mandala of Saturn is fifteen hundred thousand [yojanas] above that;
and the mandala of the Seven Sages is twenty-six hundred thousand [yojanas] above that. (PS 1.12.82)
Eleven lakhs from that point is Dhruva, the beloved of Hari;
he is situated upon the great wheel-mark on the tail of Viṣṇu’s Śiṃśumāra form.
The illustrious Viṣṇu fashioned all the planets, beginning with Dhruva, from excellent Vāruṇa wood;
he, the glorious one, triumphs with them joined to the holes of the spokes on both sides.
For all these move in regions equal to those of the sun, each subsequent one by means of cords established upon the feet of the stars, measured accordingly.
The Lord coordinates time through the movements of these zodiacal signs;
the moon traverses the twelve signs in the course of one month.
Mars, having traversed a sign in half a month, will reach the next sign;
Jupiter in twelve months, and Saturn in thirty months.
In just one month, Mercury and Venus fully occupy each zodiac sign; the Moon and Sun, however, always move at equal speed, while the two [other planets] are characterized by retrogression and voids.
The moon, moving within the solar disc, may be visible or set;
likewise, the five [planets] beginning with Mars, following the sun, will set.
When Venus and Jupiter have set in the eastern quarter, they are considered to have risen in the western quarter;
when those two have set in the western quarter, they are considered to have risen in the eastern quarter.
In this way, others also say that the setting of the sun does not occur by its own nature;
rather, they say the sun has set when it has come into the shadow of Mount Meru.
One should abandon auspicious activities during the worldly eclipses of the moon and sun;
likewise, when Venus has set in the eastern direction and remains so for two months.
The poetic [knowledge] that has set in the west rises fully again within seven days;
the teacher [knowledge] rises within a month; indeed, in both cases, it certainly becomes manifest.
The various movements of Mars and the other planets— such as retrograde, initial obstruction, direct, and swift— are indicators of inauspicious time.
Their course is not uniform; their meeting occurs only at certain times, like those placed upon a hundred-thousand-year-long yoke by means of a cord.
Indeed, the seven horses of the Sun, which bear one-twelfth of its burden,
revolve around Mānasottara, which extends for ninety million [yojanas].
Those of great speed join together to perform circumambulation;
thus the Supreme Person [is] the Kālacakra with the nine planets.
By the movement of the sun, Hari designates the months beginning with Meṣa according to the solar measure;
and by the movement of the moon, he designates those beginning with Caitra.
They calculate the lunar months from the sequence of the constellations; they determine the revolution, the attainment of the four [periods], and the movements and measurements of Jupiter.
The Gāndharvas consider the Sarasvata measure to consist of fortnights, days, and nights;
indeed, the wise declare that the Sarasvata is the standard of the Gāndharvas.
The wise know that a month [of mortals] constitutes a day and night by the measure of Mitra;
and by a period of time equal to that many years, one day and night of the gods is reckoned.
Manu is the authority known as the Mānava, while the Brahma-measure belongs indeed to the Unborn;
and Viṣṇu alone is the originator of the nine measures of measurement.
In the center of the Ocean of Milk, which is thirty-two lakhs in extent, there is a circular wall whose width and height are half that [measure].
Ten lakhs of yojanas above the earth is Śvetadvīpa, whose essence is Ramā;
its inhabitants possess the color of the Vedas, and space and time are eternally pervaded there, being regarded as insentient.
Wind, space, and solar radiance are non-eternal and considered insentient;
they are substances that do not offer resistance to one another and serve as mutual supports.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are of the nature of pure consciousness, their forms all-pervasive;
and there are three [realms], such as Śvetadvīpa, where there is no obstruction to any object.
The worlds, moreover, are unimpeded, yet they appear as worldly forms due to the obstructions of pillars and the like;
above that is the region of the Durgās, and above that is the region of the earth.
Śrībhāga is above that, and Śikhara is situated above it;
in all three parts, the earth-roots (bhūkanda) are ten thousand [yojanas] high and five hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent.
In each of the three parts, Ramā exists in the form of the region, the palace, and the ground;
the palace, the region, and the portions of earth have a bulbous foundation (*kanda*) of one hundred thousand *yojanas*.
The upper portion of the two volutes consists of three parts equal to the earth-kanda;
and within those three parts, the pillars rest upon a jeweled ground-surface.
Measuring two hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas] and adorned with various jewels,
the Lord of Lakṣmī, Anantabhānu, dwells upon a central altar situated in the middle of Śrībhaga.

The abode of Viṣṇu, consisting of pure consciousness, infinite, liberated, and worshipful, exists above heaven; it is the three-footed station of Viṣṇu situated in the elevated region of the celestial heaven.
The portion belonging to Durgā in Śvetadvīpa is two hundred and eighty thousand [yojanas],
while the terrestrial portion is half of that, and the portion belonging to Śrī is half of that again.
The inner portions of their bodies were like walls blazing with jewels and gold;
they were adorned with many archways, watchtowers, pedestals, and courtyards.
They are crowded with jewel-filled rivers, mountains, lakes, ponds, and so forth; they are radiant with the waters of various aquatic creatures and golden lotuses.
There were golden trees with foliage rich in flowers of every season,
resounding with the calls of swans, cuckoos, peacocks, parrots, and other birds.
They are filled with various animals such as exceedingly beautiful lions and other beasts, and contain many pavilions constructed from jewels of indescribable splendor.
Endowed with various delightful sounds, it was filled with throngs of men and women,
and resounded with the songs and melodies of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
There are the sounds of various musical instruments, great lutes, conchs, and drums;
and there are the emblems of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, banners, parasols, and so forth.
Richly adorned with all kinds of ornaments and garments, crowded with rows of celestial palaces,
providing the means for various sports, and enhanced by diverse fragrances.
There are couches covered with many swan-feathers and spread with jeweled sheets,
surrounded by women for pleasure, and provided with jeweled fans and mirrors.
They are adorned with various implements such as walls and vessels made of jewels and gold, and with all kinds of unmentioned accessories in infinite variety.
They were provided with yak-tail whisks, swinging cradles, footstools, and other furnishings,
and were adorned with garlands of *tulasī* flowers, excellent jewels, and pearls.
Blazing with the radiance of ten million suns, she takes the form of the sacrificial vessel and the food offering;
she consists of the substances of ghee, curd, and water, and her essential nature is that of the previously mentioned objects.

She who is the sovereign of all things, appearing in the form of a wife amidst a multitude of male and female servants; she who exists as Durgā, the Earth, and Śrī, manifesting in infinite and endless forms within her own portions.
He constantly worships the Lord Viṣṇu, who is of infinite form;
for him, no object whatsoever is expected to be attained through his very nature alone.
Hari, whose desires are fulfilled, the unborn one, accepts that worship with affection;
for in all three states, that Goddess is the embodiment of the meaning spoken by Ananta.
In all places and at all times, Ramā is the one who rests upon every form.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
"Those who were described as gods, Gandharvas, and those skilled in ritual action are non-ultimate (atāttvika)."
Those who possess the qualification for the state of the Perfected (pakva) depart from the earth and proceed to the worlds beginning with Mahar.
Established by means of the path taught in the *Vipaśeṣa*, they abide in their own superior [worlds],
yet remain fixed within the bodies and enjoyments [of the realm] up to the stainless ground at the end of the egg.
Having abandoned their marks by the power of the fourth state, when the destruction of the egg has arrived,
they enter the womb of the Sun during the time remaining after one-eighth of the day has passed.
Even those who have been liberated are not called "liberated" again once the cosmic egg comes into being,
for they have gone outside Viṣṇu’s belly with bodies composed of pure *sattva*.
Those residing in Śvetadvīpa quickly reach Hari by means of the previously mentioned infinite, pure, and enjoyable objects granted by Ramā.
Having seen, bowed to, and propitiated the Lord, and having obtained the name "Mukta" by His command,
they possess unimpeded movement toward their desired goal in Vaikuṇṭha along with the pure *sāttvika* beings.

Those who are adorned with the splendor of Śrī rejoice in both the earth and the mountain regions with bodies of hair; however, in the realm of Śrī, those whose bodies consist of pure consciousness do not abide here as inert matter.
For trees, birds, and wild animals, as well as oceans, rivers,
and lakes of various kinds— even those bound within the worlds— belong indeed to Hari.
Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā— these serve Hari directly,
desiring an increase in their own bliss for the sake of achieving their own preeminence.
Indeed, they dwell in the realm of experience solely with their subtle bodies (*liṅgadeha*);
for those who are partless, their subtle bodies reside within the cosmic egg in Satyaloka. (They indeed dwell upon the surface of the earth. PS_1,13.10.
For [the elements] arise from Aniruddha after a brief interval; since their dissolution occurs prior to the destruction of the Egg, that destruction would not belong to the subtle body.
Beginning from grass up to all the mortal Gandharvas,
the creation of their subtle bodies proceeds in sequence; therefore, it is appropriately called "the weighing" (atolaya).
Having created within these very [beings] the deities beginning with the immortal Gandharvas and ending with those of action,
they indeed become endowed with the subtle state through Nīrūddha, who abides in the portion of Durgā.
Dissolution occurs in the reverse order of creation;
when Hari has entered therein, these [elements] exist as mere subtle bodies even before the destruction of the cosmic egg.
Indeed, grasses and other impure things dwell upon the ground,
whereas the river Virajā, which serves as the moat for the region of Śrī, exists within its waters.
For those whose lingas were previously shattered by the destruction of the cosmic egg and who have attained refuge in the Fourth State (turya),
their dwelling shall be within the womb of Śrī Hari.
But those departing from the earth, having abandoned their bodies, ascend through Mahas, Janas, Tapas, and Satya— low and high respectively— in the region known as Durga.
Those who are without parts dwell through their bodies and enjoyments; indeed,
they become withered by enjoyment, for they are [bound] by Aniruddha.
For those who have entered into Aniruddha indeed enter into Saṅkarṣaṇa for the sake of victory over him.
Therefore, those who have been released from the subtle body (liṅga) arise as non-real;
having entered into superior bodies for the sake of experience, they indeed come into being.
Kubera is indeed the lord of the Gandharvas, and Yama is the lord of the Pitṛs;
likewise, he is the lord of the seventy million species across all classes, including the cowherd girls whose bodies were drawn to his touch.

In the realm of the Lord of Wealth (Dhanādhipa), there are one hundred minus one hundred crores (i.e., zero) of sages equal to him, along with their wives, who are born of the natural order (*ājāna*). PS_1,13.22 //

Indeed, at the dissolution of these [deities] who are equal to Dakṣa, the dissolution of the group of Agni’s sons and of the gods born of ritual action (karmaja) into the fire is held to occur during the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara].
In that [system], eleven are considered the Anavas;
two are the Tātvikas, namely those who are the lords of Manu at the beginning of the seventh [kalpa].
Nārāyaṇa himself is Viṣṇu, who is proclaimed as the Tāpasa Manu;
without those three Manus, dissolution is said to occur during the Svāyambhuva period.
The first was Indra; then Hariyajña, Vāyu, Dharma, and the Aśvins in succession;
the sixth was named Mandradyumna, and the seventh was Purandara.
Two are portions of Śacī’s husband; these six are remembered as the real [Indras].
The future Indras are born of karma; among them, the dissolution of the first occurs in fire.
The dissolution of seven hundred ṛṣis is recorded to occur within Dakṣa and Dharma, as well as for an equal number of the seven classes of ancestors.
There are eight gandharvas equal to him and eighty daughters, headed by Urvaśī;
indeed, those equal to her enter into Kubera.
Therefore, for yogins, the departure from the body is partless and supreme;
however, for others who depart from the world of mortals to go to the Mahar-loka and other realms, that departure is not ultimately real.
For when consumed by excellent bodies that grant enjoyments, they indeed become powerful;
then the yogis sang of them in both ascending and descending order.

Having abandoned the gross [body] for the sake of the subtle on the earth, those who are eternally transmigrating enter into dharma; indeed, they become those who have not yet abandoned primordial ignorance.
Some are liberated right here; some on the peak of Mount Meru;
or in Vaiśvānara, or in the celestial river, or in the sun, or even in the body itself.
Having abandoned ignorance at the navel, the abode of mixed fruition,
those who have gone to Hari wander through the creations of heaven, earth, and so forth, by the will of Śrī Hari.
Having been rendered unworthy by the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa arising from the womb,
they dwell in the eternal hell of Pātāla with their subtle bodies shattered.
By the blow of Vāyu’s mace, their lingas shattered,
those followers of Tamas fall by the will of Śrī Hari into the darkness at the time of dissolution and creation.
The gods, who possess conceit regarding reality, [abide] internally and externally as subtle atoms;
they do not transmigrate into those superior to them, because of their specific paths such as the *vipaśeṣa*.
Having abandoned their gross bodies, they indeed dwell in Satyaloka with their subtle bodies;
when Satya is destroyed, those born from the lotus perish along with them in the body of Brahmā.
When the egg has dissolved away, [the soul] attains a specific state together with those who have gone there,
remaining in that place with subtle bodies, along with all the subtle beings residing therein.
In this way, even the twenty-one groups of principles become unified;
however, in the reverse order, there is a collection of the principles beginning with the earth element.

Likewise, when [the body] is on land and under the control of Nābhimānin, Viṣṇu, along with the gods, [bestows] food and so forth; above that, by the sequence of ascending [levels], [it is governed] by the deities named after those [elements].
Having abandoned other obscurations, these [obstacles] go toward destruction through the previously mentioned method of pride,
in sequence, like Aniruddha and others.
When all subtle bodies have been completely destroyed by Saṅkarṣaṇa, then half of the sattva element, consisting of the portions of Śrī, Bhaga, Lakṣmī, and Alakṣmī, remains in the water. 43.
(Meaning: into the Virajā river at Pradhāna,) those whose *liṅgas* have been shattered by the lower wheel enter the belly of Hari;
and when the cosmic egg has arisen again, they reach completion in Śvetadvīpa. (PS 1.13.44)
Upon liberation, that world situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk,
called Puṣkara, becomes vast, extending for sixty-four lakṣas [of yojanas] through the splendors of Lakṣmī.
The continent, encircled by the Ocean of Milk, possesses the luster of jewels and diamonds;
in its center stands the circular Mānasottara mountain.
Elevated by as many yojanas as there are mountains on earth, two thousand yojanas in width,
firm and composed of diamond— there stands the seven-wheeled chariot of the Sun.
Within that is the mortal cycle of existence, and outside of it is the domain of mortals,
surrounded by an ocean of pure water equal in extent to the continents.
Surrounding that as well is the auspicious golden ground, coated with diamond paste, measuring nine hundred and ninety-six lakhs [yojanas] in extent; situated upon it is the mountain.
The great mountain named Lokāloka is circular in shape, encircling [the world];
it consists of jewels and gold, is pure, and stands like a rampart.
It is fifty thousand [yojanas] in width and fifty lakhs in extent;
it is raised by that same amount, and from there it rises an additional half-lakh.
Therein the world, as previously described, shines supported by various trees;
and its peaks in the eight directions are likewise perforated with openings.
Hundreds of tusker-elephants of the quarters stand upon it;
encircling its openings with their trunks, they prop it up with those very trunks.
And in the *gotrānta*, those auspicious ones situated in the sky, possessed by the descent of Hari,
have arrived upon the earth from within the cosmic egg (*garbhoda*) in the eight directions beginning with the east.
By the will of Śrī Hari, they remain on Mount Mānasottara, on Meru, and in heaven, having assumed other forms, holding aloft various objects with their own hands.
The mounts of the world-protectors carry out the command of Śrī Hari;
the Blessed One, with infinite forms, moves above that mountain.
Hari, whose upward-reaching summit touches the infinite above,
[pervades] the light of the sun, moon, stars, and planets within the interval between the Lokāloka mountain and the world beyond.

They say that in the eastern continents, [the teachings] of Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Atri, and others extend to infinity, reaching as far as the golden land, just as the sun rises within the eastern regions.
Just so, on a mountain peak, those led by Maitreya said that beyond the Golden Land (Svarṇabhūmi) stood that most excellent of mountains.
Regarding this, the followers of Paiṅgi and others have said [one thing], while Mṛkaṇḍaja has said "no";
however, Meru is a triangular region situated between Lokāloka and the world.
It is proclaimed that its extent, including the Lokāloka mountain range, measures nine million yojanas in circumference.
Surrounding that mountain is the Andhatamas hell, extending for seventy million leagues,
where those possessed of false knowledge fall by the hundreds of millions.
Those who hate Hari, the preceptor of the gods, Viṣṇu, and the Vaiṣṇavas; those who, without cause, revile holy men, women, the Vedas, and the scriptures; PS 1.13.62.
Devoid of even a fraction of devotion, they are intent upon daily and occasional rites,
yet remain entirely free from even a trace of fear regarding the commission of endless sins.
The non-difference of souls, the state of being devoid of qualities, as well as the possession of incomplete qualities,
and the difference regarding equality or superiority among others— all that pertains solely to Him.
Perversion regarding manifestation, hatred toward its devotees, and disparagement of its authority—all these are considered forms of hatred. (PS 1.13.65)
Having obtained birth in Bhārata as a result of the ripening of hatred toward Viṣṇu and other such acts,
they experience a corresponding perversion due to their enmity toward the indirect Guru.

Having cast aside their own accumulated merit due to an aversion to the nature of what has ripened, those who act with negligence have experienced the full fruit of their difficult-to-avoid *prārabdha* karma and have passed away. (PS 1.13.67)
The fruit of karma already well-commenced is diminished by hatred toward Viṣṇu; having experienced that, one must indeed cast off future karma produced by the ripening of such hatred.
Those called Nityatāmisra desire to obtain the suffering of casting off their gross bodies through poison, fire, weapons, and various forms of torment.
Before the destruction of the egg, having cast off the subtle bodies there,
the breaking of the *liṅga* will occur due to the blow of the mace from Vāyu.
The wicked, who for a long time have experienced suffering in the region of the belly of the illustrious Hari,
fall utterly once more into the blinding darkness when the cosmic egg is produced again.
The lowest mortals are partless *piśācas* with very slight *tamas*; among them, some in the lower realms possess forms that are reflections of the true deities.
Wandering through the heavens and other realms, those Daityas and Rākṣasas, who pride themselves on their evil deeds, possess various portions and assume many forms.
Previously, while residing in the netherworld (rasātala), they had resorted to subtle bodies;
then, by the power of their karma, they obtained gross bodies along with the great asuras.
Having perished themselves, they destroy other virtuous people by means of fallacious proofs;
like those standing on a high spot above a place sunken by a hundred fathoms in blind darkness.
They experience the suffering they have earned in pure forms of darkness,
amidst pus, blood, urine, excrement, and the like, as well as heated oil, missiles, and weapons.

Through various terrible calamities such as thunderbolts, which are brought about by difficult paths and unsuitable objects that lead to the acquisition of suffering never before seen or heard; PS_1,13.77.
Possessing a form corresponding to that of lions, tigers, and other such creatures,
the wind will inflict upon them an immeasurable flood of suffering.
They say that what is to be attained is suffering already ordained, even more so than that;
they experience everything from all diseases and wounds while remaining in their own true nature.
Constantly undergoing all manner of wounds and the like, they experience complete suffering; beyond that,
at a distance of fourteen million [yojanas],
stands the Ghanoda ocean surrounding it.
There, the Lord of Śrī, whose nature is the form of the infinite body of Nārāyaṇa,
always sports with Śrī, served even by Brahmā and the other gods.
Above that, at a height of ten million [yojanas], is the seat of Ananta belonging to the Lord;
it has an altar twenty hundred thousand [yojanas] high, touched by the rim of the vessel of the world-sphere.
The area of the ground is proclaimed to measure forty lakhs [yojanas], while its height is thirty lakhs; this glorious region is auspicious in every respect.
Multiplied by infinite factors beyond that, it is remembered as being equal to Śvetadvīpa.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
Beneath the earth are Talātala, Vitala, and then Sutala.
Ayuta is the extent of Unnāha; Talātala and Mahātala [are each ten thousand yojanas].
Rasātala and Pātāla lie below this;
they are two thousand [yojanas] apart, like the roots of the earth, each resembling a subterranean cavity.
Illuminated by the light of great jewels and free from the sun and other planets, Mount Meru stands to their north; this path is recognized everywhere.
In all of them, there were trees equal to the wish-fulfilling kalpavṛkṣa,
cows equal to the wish-granting kāmadhenu, and rocks equal to the cintāmaṇi jewel.

To those residing there, whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous, [the trees] bestow their fruit as is appropriate; and even their pure water becomes auspicious according to the specific nature of each person.
Therein, happiness does not come from exertion; rather, it brings happiness without effort, being filled with a vast multitude of objects enjoyed at will.
As long as there is merit resulting from desire, so long does life exist for the virtuous; however, for those who are not virtuous, it is below.
Those who dwell in Bhārata on earth during the Kṛta age are recorded as having a lifespan of one hundred thousand years.

In the three ages beginning with Tretā, human beings have lifespans measured by a reduction of one-tenth [of the previous]; they are characterized by such things as mental anguish, physical disease, decrepitude, exhaustion, and so forth.
Because lifespan is fixed according to the age (yuga), there is indeed no such thing as death at an untimely hour there;
nor is there anywhere any attachment or aversion toward those residing there, whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous, except for devotion.
Likewise, there are neither injunctions nor prohibitions, nor the [distinctions of] castes, stages of life, and so forth;
there, neither ritual action nor knowledge, nor all those who enjoy the fruits of prior karma exist.
The portions of Prāya were born from him upon the earth as the lords of the ordinances (Brahmā and Śiva),
through the boons granted by Viṣṇu and Vāyu, who had descended as incarnations to subdue the enemies of the gods.

Those who have died among them return once more to their former state—whether it be one involving *prārabdha* or *kāmya* karma—and experience the auspicious results; however, for those whose actions were free from desire (*niṣkāmya*), there is never any inauspiciousness whatsoever.

Those who have committed sinful acts out of desire become hell-beings; those who perform inauspicious acts without desire become spirits (tanū); those who desire [enjoyment] internally become Daityas; and those who have earned merit through the Bharata [lineage] become partless beings (niraṃśa).
By their own desire, the Dānavas, who were the source of prosperity for those [regions], dwelt there;
Śeṣa and the others always reside there when there is a cause.
The gods dwell there by the will of Hari, not by the force of their karma;
for these worlds are situated below the center of the bulbous root of the earth.
In Pātāla, twenty-eight hells have been created by Hari;
beneath that lies the pure water of the cosmic womb, extending for twenty-five koṭis.
There, where the Lord of Lakṣmī shines in the form of a youth,
he dwells upon a single head of the thousand-headed serpent.
To the Lord of Vāruṇī, this entire universe is indeed like a mustard seed;
so too is this whole earth, with its continents, oceans, and mountain ranges.
Its support is the wind-turtle; its form is that of the tortoise Hari.
The Śakti, abiding in the midst of the water and having the form of the support, sustains that.
The self of Saṅkarṣaṇa-Nṛsiṃha is named Ananta, the destroyer;
below him is the frog, and below that is the bank of the Varāha.
They say that beneath them is the world of the Pātālas, touched by the rims of their egg-shaped shells;
above those is the world of the earth (Bhūrloka), and in its center stands Mount Meru.
He has the appearance of a lotus stalk rising from the navel of the one whose navel is like a lotus;
he is the light arising from the center of Meru, taking refuge in the six lotuses above.
Extending one hundred yojanas in width and reaching as far as the end of Satyaloka in length,
its interior was made luminous by a cavity that was exceedingly firm due to being composed of diamond.

The Bhuvarloka rests upon the earth at a height of one hundred thousand yojanas; it is composed of jewels and gold, measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, and is the delight of the world, beautiful as a realm.
It is encircled by seven walls and filled with various enjoyments and great yogis,
as well as with insentient objects abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva) and possessing pure abodes.
Extending ten million yojanas in width, like the Bhuvarloka, it is as delightful as the heavenly realm rising ten million leagues above the earth and is perfectly circular.
Supported by two hundred thousand earth-roots, it rests upon the stalk of Mount Meru;
it is radiant with seven lofty walls made of jewels and gold.
The well-arranged avenues were ten yojanas in width and square in shape,
where many banners and numerous mirrors were densely arrayed.
Adorned with palaces born from the golden glory of their former merits, they were furnished with couches and seats of jewels and with means appropriate for those of infinite sattva.
It shone with eight gardens and eight abodes of the world-protectors in the eight directions,
with a pavilion for the temple of Viṣṇu resplendent in its center with clusters of jewels.
They are crowded with all kinds of weapons, chariots, and wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi),
and are adorned with a continuous array of all ornaments, including strings of pearls and jewels.
They are crowded with divine garments, food, and many *pārijāta* trees;
they possess twenty-eight city gates, archways, watchtowers, and gatehouses.
The rivers there flow through excellent houses surrounded by thousands of palatial mansions;
they possess lotuses whose forms are equal to those of the celestial Mandākinī and are composed of jewels.
In its form as a universal pillar (parigha), it shines there accompanied by hosts of aquatic creatures;
endowed with excellent sound, touch, and form, it possesses exquisite taste and fragrance.
The Bhuvarloka and the lower worlds are filled with various objects of enjoyment for mortals, gods, and asuras,
each increasing a hundredfold in quality over the one before it.
From that, the worlds beginning with heaven increase tenfold in succession;
likewise, the continuous lineages of gods and asuras residing in those respective worlds [increase accordingly].

The imperishable Viṣṇu will provide a support for those of limited intellect— such as gods with specific offices, virtuous mortals, Gandharvas, and others— granting each of them their appropriate fruit.
Beyond that, Maharloka, which is devoid of karma, stands at a height of one and a half koṭis;
above that, Janaloka, which is highly honored, is situated at a height of two koṭis.
Beyond that is the world of heat (tapoloka), two and a half crores [yojanas] high and accessible to those of pure conduct;
beyond that is this radiant world of truth (satyaloka), one crore [yojanas] in height.
The sphere of knowledge [is reached] from the earth-center at three, four, five, or six hundred thousand [yojanas],
rising from the navel to the tip of the great stalk situated in the realm of Satyaloka.
Brahmā, the creator of all worlds, was born four-faced by Viṣṇu;
the specific purposes of the heavenly worlds are continuously maintained within the Maharloka and the other realms.
In the final half of the lifespan, such a worldly state will arise, serving as a refuge for various hosts of mortals.
There, at the beginning of the day, Hari creates the world consisting of those possessed of ego through the primordial nature (prakṛti);
this world of the Unborn is considered to measure thirteen crores of yojanas.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā: Śrī Haṃsa said— above twelve crores from Satyaloka is the world named Vaikuṇṭha.
The lower region is the portion of Durgā; it is the root of the earth, measuring ten lakhs [yojanas].
Above that is the region of earth, and above that is the region of Śrī;
these three are equal to the root of the earth (bhūkanda) and are measured at thirty lakhs [of yojanas] in height.
On three parts of that peak are many great palaces,
composed of jewels, numbering eight, and auspicious.
In the center is a single vajra-throne, and there are also the four surrounding enclosures, such as the Great Wall and so forth, extending for a hundred yojanas in width.
Just as the worlds [are situated] within the three divisions, so too are the Vaikuṇṭha realms;
they touch the shell of the cosmic egg and, in their midst, consist of seven enclosures.
Arranged with doors facing the east and other directions, there are seven golden [palaces] each, with door-panels made of emerald and ruby.
Resplendent with vajra-bands upon thighs as dark as sapphires,
their elevated flanks were like altars of shimmering gems, glowing on both the right and left sides.
At every gate there are halls provided with noble thrones made of jeweled lotuses,
adorned with ornaments that beautify the world and blaze with the infinite light of the sun.
In each of those three parts, she who assumes infinite and boundless forms dwells together with Brahmā and all the lords of the gods.
The vision of the three regions beginning with Vaikuṇṭha certainly occurs;
however, they do not have a permanent residence there, for their abode is in the Mahar-loka and the worlds above it.
Grass and other such things exist in Maharloka; humans and others exist above that;
kings exist in Tapoloka; and human-like beings exist in Satyaloka.

For those who are liberated, as well as for those who are bound, there is departure [from the body] and abiding here; those ending with humans, gandharvas, and ājānajās have departed, while those established in austerity abide here.
For the karma-devas, having ascended, dwell in Satyaloka; though they have reached the three stages, they are unreal and liberated from the subtle body (liṅga).
Indeed, it does not stand upon the rampart within the three parts;
rather, the ramparts are situated outside the Śrī-bhāga above that.
Surrounding that [central palace], which consists of four sides,
there is an outer wall described as having twelve sides and being joined with watchtowers.
Within that are six walls, providing space for intervals between them;
above that, there is an outer enclosure consisting of eight corners.
The auspicious river named Virajā, extending for ten million yojanas, is the Śrī;
indeed, by the mere touch of its waters, beings become liberated from the subtle body (liṅga) immediately.

There, the people constantly resorted to Hari, who was devoted to sporting in the water; he was the one who removed the burden of the earth, while the earth itself was the refuge for those seeking shelter.
In the middle of that, on the ground consisting of the glorious portion elevated by one hundred thousand [yojanas], there is Virajā;
therein are two auspicious portions, the abodes of the liberated and the unliberated.
Thus, when situated on a difficult portion, it is joined with the surrounding environment;
the two portions of the ground are difficult, while the middle portion of the earth has a raised form.
Above those two are the rivers named Ūrdhvāraṇa and Tassandhi; they are difficult to traverse, consist of water, and are dear to Śrī Hari.
In that place, Hari never even considered the destruction of gender and so forth;
between Pradhāna and the supreme ether lies the Virajā river.
Those two, Brahmā and Vāyu, together with their wives and possessing bodies composed of *pradhāna*,
reside above and below the terrestrial region during the dissolution, along with all the gods.
Except for the Suras, at the beginning and at the conclusion of the incarnations,
[the earth and the sky] may, by the will of Hari, at certain times, move upward from their respective positions on the ground.
Therefore, the region above the earth is proclaimed to be the primary [element].
Whatever depends on something for its existence is said to be that very thing. (PS 1.15.25)
The venerable portion, being conjoined with such a primary matter (pradhāna), is the supreme ether;
therefore, it is designated as "the one who has transcended the primary matter" (vyomaga).
Furthermore, for those who are not ultimately real, there is immersion within the cosmic egg;
however, for all those who are ultimately real, they remain within the covering of Aniruddha.
When the impurity has been established on a high place for the sake of the protection of sentient beings,
it becomes unified within the beautiful abodes of Śvetadvīpa.
When Śrī, Durgā, and Bhūmi have become one in the hundred-thousand-fold [digit], that is the portion of Śrī;
therein lies his enclosure, the river Virajā.
Then, having bathed in that water, the dissolution of the linga is seen for the virtuous ones who, at the time of the world's dissolution, are departing by transcending the earthly covering.
The first enclosure has been described; the final one is the enclosure of sentient beings.
That which is unmanifest space is called by the word "void" (vyoman).
Because it is stainless and situated between the infinite [consciousness] and the sky of the veil,
its arising within the limbs of the deities is held to be union with their limbs. (PS 1.15.32)
In the infinite form of the illustrious Bhagavat Vaikuṇṭha, that Vāsudeva who bears the discus,
there shall be complete union (sāyujya) with Brahman for all limbs.
Furthermore, for one who is liberated, an increase in the size of the atom in its essential nature is not logical;
nor is there any decrease, nor the recurrence of suffering, ignorance, fear, and so forth. (PS 1.15.34)
For those who are extremely lowly and have little renunciation, fulfillment comes from their own pleasure alone;
they have no desire for the highest joy, which is the fruit of service, meditation, and so forth.
For Hari, as for others, his own arms are not merely arms;
indeed, at the proper time, dissolution and creation reside solely within His glorious being.
Brahmā, whose body consists of pure consciousness alone, is considered to reside within the innermost enclosure;
Rudra and the others occupy the sixth enclosure, while Indra and the others are situated in the fifth.
The deities beginning with Sūrya are situated in the fourth enclosure; the hosts of Maruts are in the third;
and the supreme gods beginning with Parjanya are stationed in the second enclosure.
In the first Śrībhāga, those whose bodies consist of pure consciousness are preceded by the fruits of their karma;
however, these same liberated ones reside in the Bhūbhāga and likewise in the Durgābhāga.
Those who have attained the bodies of pure *sāttvika* beings have reached the happiness of Hari;
indeed, they constitute more than eighty-four hundred thousand among the multitude of living beings.
The Self in the form of the image, eternally residing therein, protects all the hosts of living beings who are liberated in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.

For Hari, the all-pervading Lord, is indeed the protector even of living beings; he exists through various forms— some minute and equal to all living beings, and others such as these, which are gross.
Having been worshipped for infinite millions of eons, he has transcended the three realms;
endowed with such infinite splendor, he moves together with her.
There, those two are the bestowers of infinite and boundless objects suitable for worship;
there, by means of the implements such as the crown representing one's own essential nature, and the conch, discus, and so forth, [they grant these fruits].

He was personally worshipped with his own forms, using weapons such as the Sudarśana, as well as offerings of perfumes, garlands, and the like, along with food offerings, garments, beds, and other articles.
Having attained complete identity with Śrī, he rejoices in the form of bliss;
Śrī, the goddess who possesses all forms, thoroughly worships Viṣṇu through them. (PS 1.15.46)
By means of those flower-garlands offered to Viṣṇu, one clearly becomes one with Rama;
likewise, through these pure sāttvika practices, one attains union in both the earth and the fortress regions.
Having worshipped Brahmā and the other gods with the remains of that [offering], Śrī, who considers herself their equal, grants liberation;
O wise ones, she then gratifies them with auspicious perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Those celestial chariots and swings, with their hair-ornaments swaying like cradles,
were sometimes filled with beds, ornaments, garments, and the like, as well as elephants, lions, and other creatures.
Together with their equals and superior people, using fruits, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth,
as well as water-sports and other such activities with their respective beloved young women.
Even all those who possess unimpeded and desired modes of movement bow down with worship, through noble discourses and other means, being themselves free from rebirth.
Indeed, there are ninety million hosts of deities established in the [nine] stations;
all of them, together with their wives, possess bodies that are subtle, gross, and characterized by the *liṅga*.
Indeed, they dwell perfectly in the portion of Durgā for the sake of serving Śrī Hari,
[providing] with those things produced from the wish-fulfilling cow, the kalpa-tree, and the cintāmaṇi gem.
[He should worship] with water offered by Śrīkara, joined with the objects of the yoga of the infinite [deities],
and with the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Hari that have been used for worship and then returned.
With their limbs purified on all sides, they wander about joyfully,
[attaining] eternal union with Hari, as well as residence in his realm, and proximity to him.
Indeed, liberation is said to be of four kinds, including sārupya;
for Viṣṇu [resides] within the bodies of the liberated ones, who enjoy solely their own individual bliss.
For that indeed brings about union (*sāyujya*) with those gods, while for the *karmadevas*, the three states beginning with proximity (*sāmīpya*) are sometimes applicable. (PS 1.15.57)
For those divine servants distinct from him, the two [liberations] beginning with sā rūpya (having the same form) are considered;
while for the other, it is known as sālokya (residing in the same world). (PS 1.15.58)
If those endowed with four arms, wearing yellow garments and slightly smiling, appear within pure *sāttvika* bodies, it is described as *sārūpya*.
Jaya and Vijaya, Bala and likewise Prabala,
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, as well as Nanda and Sunandaka.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, as well as Bhadra and Subhadraka,
and those named Sudhāman and Dāman, abide under the command of Viṣvaksena.
All of them, moreover, are endowed with four forms; they stand in the seven locations within the four directions, beginning from the gate leading to the inner enclosure, acting as gatekeepers.
Nandinī rises from the foot of Hari; Durgā and Bhāgā have auspicious waters.
That [region] is Parighā, and Vaikuṇṭha is proclaimed to be square.
In the world of Viṣṇu, who pervades the entire cosmic egg, there is a realm named Vaikuṇṭha;
it is conceived as being upon the face, that is, the head, of Him whose infinite heads rise up for ten million yojanas.
The feet are the sandals untouched by the skull-cup situated within the waters of the womb;
the hips are known as the seat of Ananta, whose nature is the yellow garment.
The Ghanodaka ocean is at the waist, with Mount Meru situated in its central navel;
it extends twenty-five koṭis of yojanas from Mount Meru.
The shell of the cosmic egg is known to extend in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as above and below,

the earth, consisting of the bulb of Durgā, is in the center in the form of a stalk.

Above that, in the auspicious portion, the altar (vedikā) is considered to be situated in the third part, having the nature of the lotus of Ramā, measuring one and a half finger-breadths and being firm.
That pavilion was made of jewels, possessed four doors, and was a beautiful abode;
it was enchanting with fragrant scents, jewel-lamps, and plantain-tree pillars.
Adorned with archways, full water-jars, banners, and parasols,
as well as jeweled pillars, pearl necklaces, and various white sprouts.
The venerable portion is the honor of the lotus; he himself is Hari, known as Mūleśa.
Above the lotus, the maṇḍalas of the moon, sun, and fire are clearly manifest.
The divine couch, with its lovely pillows, was indeed beautiful;
upon it sat Hari, whose form remained as a mere semblance, with his hoods raised high.
Above that is Ramā, whose form is a variegated throne; she moves above him.
He, however, is the Prājña-ātman, the Lord of the individual soul (jīva), under whose control the jīva is always.
He has four arms, holding a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus;

Adorned with a necklace, the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem resting upon his neck, and other ornaments,

Clad in yellow garments, he is graced by the beauty of his entire form; though facing every direction, he appears as if having but a single face, with eyes that are dark blue.
Joined with the lords of the station (sthāneśa) and the root (mūleśa), [the deity] is to be worshipped by those without portions (niraṃśaka).
The Śakti, whose form is the support (ādhāra), resides in the region below the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
Having meditated upon Kūrma, Śeṣa, the earth, the oceans, the continents, and the white Ramā, he reflected thus with his undivided consciousness: PS_2.3.30.
In the thighs, the palate, between the eyebrows, and in the head,
there are upward-facing lotuses of white color with twelve, sixteen, and eight petals respectively.

and Vāyu, the lord of all petals, is one-headed yet manifold in form.

Kṛkala is named Devadatta, and the Lord of the Maruts is Sūtranāman.
The Maruts, numbering seven times seven, reside even within the five hearts;

The Suṣumnā, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), is described by those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas as being the single channel, devoid of branches and the like, yet possessed of openings within the womb.

she is known as Hairaṇmayī, Vaidyutī, Vajrikā, and Bhāsvatī.
The worlds beginning with Bhūr, situated therein, are joined with their respective names;
they are the lords of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar, as well as those of Mahar and the others, in due order.
Earth, Vighneśa, Indra, Aniruddha, Kāma, Śeṣa, and the Lotus-born (Brahmā) are considered [the presiding deities] for the two hips,
the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, the two ankles, and the two feet respectively.
O Lord of Gods, the deities residing in the Atala and other regions are the attendants within the body;
they are Mitra, Agni, Astra, Pavīra, Īśa, Maya, and Yamā, in due order.
In the body as well, for one who maintains the Virāj-body, it is the same;
when Suṣumnā arises from the root region, it is like the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the ocean.
The two [channels] Piṅgalā and Iḍā are red and blue in color, situated on the right and left;
they possess openings within the womb and divide into thirty-six thousand [sub-channels].
The left channels are considered to be individually composed of the principle of Mahat;
divided into three parts, they extend to the feet and are measured at twelve thousand [units].

On the right side, extending to the end of the right foot, there are channels of that same measure in sequence; likewise, the auspicious Piṅgalā channels extend upward through the body to that same extent.
These seven apertures, located in the nose, mouth, ears, and eyes, extend downward, inward, and upward, and they constitute his seven openings. (PS 2.3.45)
Seven spheres named after the seven apathas are proclaimed;

Furthermore, from the upper region, the Piṅgalā winds, having turned around the right side of the heart,
proceed there along seven paths; [therein reside] Sūrya, Vahni, and the others who are the lords of the years.

The lords of the months of the northern course, the lords of the days, and those belonging to the bright fortnight— these very ones are the presiding deities (abhimānin) over the three subsequent bright fortnights in this [cycle].
The channels named after all the gods, beginning with Sūrya, are indeed Piṅgalā;
in her resides Brahmā, while the Ṛjus are those who perceive the non-manifest.

together with Bhāratī, they abide in those [channels] in twenty-six thousand forms.
Likewise, Aniruddha and Pradyumna are on the right in male form, while on the left they are in female form; they are fully present within them in those very forms.
Abiding in the nature of those two [Pāṇa]s, they are worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others;
these deities are the lords of the months of the southern solstice and the lords of the night.
The lords of the dark fortnight, Rudra and Viśeṣa, together with their wives—
all these deities are presiding over egoity (ahaṅkāra) in the Egg of Illusion (māyāṇḍa).

Vyāna, whose nature is that of the pervasive breath, resides in all the joints, while Udāna dwells in the Brahma-nāḍī.
Suṣumnā is the channel of Brahman; Samāna pervades the entire body.
Seven channels of the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) extend respectively downward, upward, and transversely.
Traversing the path of the seven-horsed course, those upward-moving channels, which are tawny like Piṅgalā,

Having again reached the path of the seven horses (the sun) in a counter-clockwise direction, one should worship, in their entirety and in sequence,

In the body, visible form is the essence of the beautiful and the ugly, perceivable by the eye;

The objects of the sense-faculties, which are not overcome by their respective measures and are not sublated by truth, are the means for speaking, taking, moving, excreting, experiencing, and so forth. (PS 2.3.72)
The five organs of action are bound to the performance of their respective functions:

Therefore, those principles— the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—

The mind is the cause of hearing; the seven [channels] reside within the body;

At the time of weakness, the channels on the left and right sides shine forth;
indeed, they manifest the arrival [of the breath] for men and women. (PS 2.3.76)

Therefore, because they are real, the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, which reside in the body and initiate both knowledge and ignorance in many [beings], are real; those who identify with them are likewise real. (PS 2.3.77)

Thus, the internal truth (or reality), which exists externally as the objective world,

Their causes, the constituent elements (mātrās), the sense organs residing therein,

therefore, it should be understood as being false, just like that silver which is illusory. (PS 2.3.92)

this entire universe is projected upon Brahman, being itself a construction of ignorance. (PS 2.3.93)

Although that Brahman is partless, it is directly veiled by the state of being the individual soul through ignorance.

Because it is produced from false ignorance, that ignorance is not said to be real;
for, by virtue of that ignorance, [the self] resides in the individual soul, yet the soul itself lacks inherent existence.
But in the case of the undifferentiated Brahman, one abides through both knowledge and ignorance;
therefore, that [cognition] which rests upon Brahman is not produced by that [empirical] knowledge or its limiting adjuncts.
Thus, through false notions of time, action, place,
and arrival, the Brahma that wanders at the end of the eon possesses the nature of the root-Brahma.
Having realized that unity there, one is not born again on earth;
for even the liberated one possesses neither ignorance, nor sense organs, nor anything else anywhere.
In the supreme Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions, oneness is indeed of this nature;
that ignorance of it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor yet something else. (PS 2.3.100)
That which is inexpressible is called liberation, which is its cessation;
they have also declared that creation and dissolution occur at all times, both past and future.
For the wise who seek the ultimate truth do not accept this evil doctrine.
Thus ends the third chapter in the second section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
The venerable Haṃsa said:
[He is] the body consisting of knowledge along with its limbs, filled with infinite qualities.
Together with their auxiliary branches, they terrify the Lord, as described in the Vedas and the scriptures.

it is constantly contemplated and worshipped by Ramā, Brahmā, and the other gods.
He is served by individual souls—both liberated and unliberated—who are distinct from Him, inferior to Him, and infinite; He pervades all that is conscious and unconscious, the Lord of Śrī.
They recognize Hari as the creator of truth and the experiencer of suffering and so forth; it is never appropriate to attribute ignorance to him in any respect whatsoever.
There is no means of valid cognition for the claim that false ignorance exists;
it is logical that the absence of knowledge is merely a collection of adventitious limiting conditions.

But when perfection and knowledge have been attained, the adjuncts associated with those [perfections and knowledge] persist; when they are perfected, there is the conjunction of ignorance for everyone else, and due to the absence of that [ignorance], it is otherwise.
Because ignorance does not exist, there is no further knower;
because ignorance does not exist, its cessation as a distinct entity is likewise nowhere to be found.
A scripture imagined through ignorance cannot cut through ignorance;
therefore, that doctrine must be rejected, for the Lord is the bestower of liberation even to one who is bound. (PS 2.4.8)
The universe is real, not false, not sublatable, and has a real cause;
established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception, the world is not superimposed. (PS 2.4.9)
The silver perceived in mother-of-pearl does not perform a causal function, whereas the world does perform a causal function;
therefore, that [example] is not applicable as an illustration.

Furthermore, in that doctrine, Brahman would lack the cause for the world's falsity because it is devoid of an illustrative example; moreover, Brahman would likewise be false because it is an object of perception. (PS 2.4.11)
That which is declared by Viṣṇu in the Vedas, such as "the ether and so forth are without measure," is not false;
nor is there any proof for the falsity asserted by logic, nor even for his own doctrine.
Knowing that the eternal Veda is not composed by any person and cannot be refuted by fallacious arguments,
the Lord Viṣṇu, through his power, awakened the knowledge of its greatness.
The Lord of the entire world is Truth; He is worshipped eternally by true living beings through the practice of true means; He is Truth itself, the bestower of liberation through Truth.
