as well as two Gandharvas who had been born on Mount Gandhamādana due to a curse.
If one were to object that [the gods] gave nectar to the sons of Kadrū, who were of evil nature, yet released their mother from slavery, let this suffice; there is nothing more to be said.
Thus addressed, he took the nectar and gave it to Tārkṣya, thereby liberating him from slavery;
and his own mother, having gone to heaven, was likewise released from servitude by the lords of the gods.
When Śakra, having cast away the *tṛṇavanta* tree and shaken off the nectar (*sudhā*), regained his sovereignty over heaven, he then spoke to Kardama.
When asked, "From where was the nectar taken? the son of Vinatā replied:
"My mother was deceived by you; therefore, you have been deceived by me."
When told "Give [it]," he was not told "Make him drink the nectar," and therefore he swallowed it;
from that time on, Garuḍa began to kill the deceitful serpents. (PS 2.4.84)
Due to his malice toward the supreme Kardama, she became afflicted with grief for her son;
those who were deceivers fell during the sacrifice, while the others were devoured by Garuḍas.
All beings live by giving him their hand when he has risen;
who, indeed, would wish to live while greedily pursuing the life of one who is innocent?
For even those who are worthy suffer pain both here and in the hereafter;
how much more so the unworthy rākṣasas, who enter into intense darkness?
In this way, for the remainder [of the yogis], through proximity, service, drinking the nectar, friendship with Garuḍa, devotion to the Lord of Śrī, and devotion to the Guru.
By virtue of their sincerity and their devotion as servants of Śakra,
those serpents disregarded their mother’s curse and attained happiness.

What is there in this world that cannot be obtained through service to Viṣṇu and his devotees? Even the abode of serpents in the great netherworld (mahātala), though it bears the weight of calamity, [is attainable].
Those of evil mind who wander among others by the grace of Śiva go [to their downfall].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā. The Blessed Lord said:
"From the netherworld of Rasātala below, there were ten billion Dānavas."
The Daityas, the Yātudhānas, the Paulomas, and the Kālakeyas.
The Nivātakavacas, the Adhīras, the Rākṣasas, the Surāṇakas, the Piśācas, the Antyajās, the Sṛkyas, the Mahākumatis (or Mahāmudis), and the Jaras.
Out of fear of the discus and even of all other fears,
those who are truly steadfast dwell there, O bull among gods.
In every successive Manvantara, throughout this entire Bhārata-varṣa, these [beings] resort to Hari as their sole refuge— whether they be gods, demons, virtuous elephants, brahmins, women, or others.

Having corrupted and caused others to fall, some whose intellects are otherwise full [of pride] dwell eternally in hell, destroyed by the gods such as Hari and others who are themselves consumed by the fire of their own arrogance.
Having resorted to Rasātala for the sake of their constant and difficult-to-accomplish rites,
they became inhabitants of the earth and brought harm to the worlds through the power of Brahmā, Rudra, and the gods.
By Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, through all their incarnations, all the remnants have been slain;
Kālā and the others dwell eternally in hell and shall indeed go to darkness.
For in that place dwells a bitch named Saramā, born from a boon of Brahmā;
she, remaining under the control of Yama, constantly terrifies the Daityas who are ever-afflicted.
When their lifespan is exhausted, the Daityas there will see the Sudarśana in a dream;
having died, they will go to hell, for it is the refuge of those belonging to that lineage.
Below that, however, in the radiant Pātāla in the northern direction,
resides Śeṣa with his thousand faces, together with all the authentic serpents.
Worshipped by all the daughters of the Nāgas in a pavilion of jewels,
he always dwells there with the gods, meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa.
Adorned with a row of crest-jewels blazing like the thousand-rayed sun,
his splendor exceeded that of ten million full autumnal moons.
Adorned with a circle of hoods beautiful with the constant flow of nectar,
the Lord is ever adorned with a single earring, radiant, holding a pestle, and accompanied by Halā.
With the splendor of the crest-jewel on his head eclipsing all other light like the radiance of the sun,
he was adorned with necklaces, anklets, bracelets, bangles, finger-rings, and so forth.
The Lord possesses a girdle, crown, sacred thread, and other ornaments resplendent with many jewels;
his sandals are covered by the gems set in the crowns of gods and asuras.
The Lord Virāj himself remains meditating on fragrant perfumes, garlands, and the like,
having restrained himself in the city of Saṃyamī in the southern region of Pātāla.
The beloved of Śyāmalā, wielder of the staff, whose vehicle is a buffalo,
the impartial Yama, lord of the departed, has the luster of a mountain of black collyrium.
Adorned with all ornaments, the King of Dharma contemplates Rāma;
and the two sons of Bhānu, Citra and Citragupta, are excellent scribes.
But by whose command the accumulation of merit and demerit arising from the *Bhārata* exists,
there the expounders of Dharma remain throughout their respective *manvantaras*.
The ṛṣis, all the gods and upadevas, and their attendants—
those with hair standing erect, odd-eyed, blue-colored, and terrifying— [are there].
Then his servants, who carry out his commands, are cruel, pitiless, and fierce; they hold nooses in their hands and wield great iron bars.
From Bhārata, sinners are bound and brought into the presence of Yama;
numbering ten lakhs, they are subjected to terrible beatings and burnings.
These evildoers are being dragged along the terrible path;
seeing them approaching, Yama, the king of the departed, wields his staff.
Then he places them upon their heads; at that time, all those embodied beings proclaim the merits and sins they have committed.
There, all those who were established in the nature of reality declared, "This is the truth"; and they recited those very words even as they were written upon leaves. (PS 2.5.25)
The best of sages declare that the fruit consists of pleasure and pain;
ten lakhs of them are the messengers of Yama in hell.
Having cast them down, they strike them according to their sins;
there, twenty hundred thousand [beings] are always possessed by diseases.
These include disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as fevers arising from the combination of humors (sannipāta),
fistula-in-ano, dysentery, vomiting, loss of appetite, and malignant ulcers.
In the vicinity of that heart which is afflicted by diseases such as consumption,
there dwell those [afflictions] that yield the fruit of evil and, in some cases, bring about the destruction of the body. (PS 2.5.29)
Dogs, snakes, scorpions, stinging insects, venomous creatures,
wild dogs, and wolves— these twenty hundred thousand are the tormentors of those fallen into hell.
These hells of many forms dwell in the netherworld (pātāla);
they are the miserable states and the hells, namely Mahāraurava and Raurava.
The hells known as Saṃghāta and Kālasūtra, those called Varca and Anirodhana,
the oil-press, boiling oil, falling from mountains, and the iron house.
[Sūcī, Agnibhūri, Nirghāta, Vakrakaṇṭaka, Dānava, Śvabhojana, Vratapana, Karkaśa, Ālimukha, and Ulbaṇa.]
They have a craving for pus, blood, urine, and excrement; they are tormented by the touch of heated weapons;
and they are struck by fragments of the Kālakūṭa fire and by all manner of falling missiles and arms.

The great burden of restraining the vital breaths, cruel venomous serpents and scorpions, the flesh of one's own limbs being torn from all parts of the body, and being cast down upon heated trees. (PS 2.5.35)
Śūlāroha, Apakarṣa, Durgandha, Rākṣasādana, Bāṇāghāta, Vaitaraṇī, Śaṅku, Mūlaka, and Karālaka. (PS 2.5.36)
[The powers of] ant and leech, vulture and heron in feeding, the two [powers of] turning and striking, and [the powers of] stone-machine and stone-eating; PS 2.5.37.
Karṇa and Pūrṇa were the two gatekeepers who performed the fastening of the bolts.
There are iron chains, heated sands, and showers of sparks that cover one.
The vital points (marmans), the joints, the protuberances, the constrictions, and so forth—
these very hundred and eight hells exist as abodes of sin.
These hells—Tāmisra and Andhatāmisra—are impermanent;
the two eternal hells therein are where those who have gone there enter into darkness by degrees.
Those gods who exist in the lower worlds throughout all the Manvantaras are devoted to their assigned duties and are devoid of any other names.
The names and forms of those unfit for this [state], as proclaimed here in every respect, were indeed previously practiced among humans in this very world; thus they are known by the name "Ajñānya."
Having abandoned all these gross things for the sake of the subtle,
those who have come under the control of their own higher wisdom go to Maharloka when that [Janaloka] passes away.
Having reached the gross [objects], one should gradually [attain] those belonging to the sages and those in the vicinity of one's own ancestors.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā. The Blessed Lord said:
"The seven worlds beginning with Atala are proclaimed as the subterranean heavens within the cavity."
Below Mount Meru, they are all for the most part crowded with those possessing knowledge.
Above these is the world of earth (bhūloka), which is considered the most obscure of all worlds;
for in that [world], in the land of Bhārata, in the city named Barhiṣmatī—
In the beginning, Svāyambhuva Manu was the husband of Śatarūpā; his lotus feet were served by many tens of millions of gods and demons.
He ruled this earth, always nourishing his subjects like a father; his daughter Devahūti, however, remained at times devoted to dharma.
Seeing her on the ground where he had fallen, the lord of the Gandharvas himself mounted her—
endowed with beauty and youth— upon his chariot.
He went there with his wife to the bank of the Sarasvatī; he approached Kardama, who was performing austerities there on the shore of Lake Bindu.
When King Manu had returned to his own city with difficulty after bestowing the holy hermitage,
that queen [took] a collection of garments and ornaments.
Having cast [her husband] into the river, she, being dispassionate, wearing bark garments and skins,
emaciated by her vows and bearing matted locks, attended upon her husband with devotion.
Having thus served her feet, she spoke to the princess; "Speak what is beneficial," the queen requested her, yet [the princess] chose [to remain silent] through the power of yoga.
It was filled with the radiance of jewels as bright as the rising sun,
provided with every kind of utensil, and abounded with birds, trees, and water.
Having himself bathed in that lake— which was golden, of black water, fragrant, and most enchanting— he shone, captivating the hearts of all.
Like the goddess Śrī herself, adorned with beauty, garments, and ornaments, she pleased him; and the sage took his delight with her for a hundred years.
Wandering upon Mount Meru and other peaks, seated in a divine celestial chariot as described, he is captivated by excellent sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and fragrances.
Thus, on the shore of Lake Bindusaras, his women remained close by as he passed the time like a single moment amidst the breezes of the spring season.
Listen always as I speak the names of their daughters:
Kalā, Anasūyā, Śraddhā, Havirbhū, Gati, and Kriyā.
Arundhatī, Cittī, Khyātī, and Kardamaputrikā were the daughters of Marīci; he gave Kalā to Marīci, and then Trayī to Anusūyā.
He gave Śraddhā to Aṅgiras, Havirbhū to Pulastya,
Gati to Pulaha, and his daughter Kriyā to Kratu.
He bestowed Arundhatī upon Vasiṣṭha and Citti upon Bhṛgu;
then, having given Khyāti to Atharvan, he became truly joyful.
Then, after sporting for a hundred years, he begot Kapila upon her;
through the power of his asceticism, O Kardama, he became Nārāyaṇa in person.
Having abandoned his celestial chariot and his wife, Kardama went to that bank of Lake Bindu to practice austerity, remaining there as a perpetual celibate student.
Having taught the truth regarding the Self alone, the sage Kapila granted liberation;
that truth known as Kapila’s teaching cuts through the knot of karma.
In this Vaivasvata interval, Kaśyapa was born from Marīci;
he [was born] into the thirteen daughters of Dakṣa, who had been reborn.
When Diti, Aditi, and the others were given to Kaśyapa,
he had the previously mentioned sons during the preceding Manvantaras.
Among the sons of Marīci, there was one named Kaśyapa;
furthermore, by another wife, he had sixty daughters born of Dakṣa.
In the subsequent Manvantaras, thirteen were given to Kaśyapa;
these, known by different names, became the Suras and Asuras.
Those previously mentioned, who accomplish their respective functions through their distinct names,
now exist in this [kalpa] under the name Kaśyapa, along with their wives, sons, and so forth.
Those whose names correspond to their functions, as previously stated, will exist in the future time;
they are the authentic ones, numbering no fewer than one hundred, as proclaimed by the sage Puṣkara.
In previous manvantaras,
the twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa became the wives of the Moon.
The lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī are the movers of the wheel of time; due to the falling of the fortnight upon Rohiṇī, the perspective regarding the others is reversed.
Due to the curse of Dakṣa, they remained childless throughout all the Manvantaras;
however, the daughters of Bhānu gave two daughters each to Bhūta, Aṅgiras, and Kṛśāśva.
Among the Bhānus and the Nakṣatras, a human being [is born]...;
indeed, four were given to Dakṣa, and ten to Dharma.
Their sons were for the most part conceited regarding their knowledge, devotion, and other qualities;
even the moon, born from the eye of Atri, was so throughout all the manvantaras.
The beloved of trees, medicinal herbs, and constellations;
the maker of night, the bearer of coolness, the remover of heat, and the constant giver of happiness.

The lord who bestows hopelessness upon the enemy, the moon whose nectar-rayed essence is consumed by the fire, born from the ocean, the brother of Śrī, the lord of the increasing digits, the moon, the kinsman of the world.
Both sons of Anasūyā, having received Dūrvāsas as their preceptor, were initiators of Yoga;
through Yoga they attained Brahman, and remained celibate students.
Datta was Nārāyaṇa in person, and Dūrvāsas was a portion of Śaṅkara;
filled with fierce anger, he was honored by Pṛthā and instructed Manu.
By him alone, being highly honored, were Karṇa and the others—Dharmaputra and his brothers—begotten;
he was entreated by Soma, Ārṣiṣeṇa, and others to accept food on the twelfth day when little remained.
Having said "Om," the king submerged himself in the Kālindī for a long time; then, by the command of the Brahmin, he broke his fast with water, desiring to accomplish his spiritual practice.
Having understood that, he then instructed the king on his duty; the king too remembered the discus of Hari previously obtained, which, having destroyed the magical creation, struck terror into it.
That rishi, having been rejected by all the lords of the world and by Viṣṇu, reached Ambarīśa; released and fed by him, he departed.
Having approached Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, that Durvāsas asked for Draupadī, saying, "Let me be given food immediately"; being satisfied by them, he departed.
Through faith, Aṅgiras obtained the teacher Agnimucyaka;
and the sons of Saṃvartaka and Agni, who were mentioned previously, became his teachers as well.
While Ucathya’s wife was pregnant, he desired her; thus, on the ground where her womb was located, Dīrghatapas, who was situated within the womb, covered her vulva with his foot.
Born from fallen semen, the sage Bharadvāja, who was supremely righteous,
was indeed protected by the Maruts in ancient times.
In the Vaivasvata Manvantara, within the Lunar dynasty known as that of Bharata,
when the lineage had become extinct, the Maruts then bestowed that [son] upon him.
Having raised up and released those who were oppressed and distressed,
he again practiced austerities for a long time, O descendant of Bharata’s lineage.
While Śantanu was performing austerities on the Gaṅgā, which had darkened the world,
Bharadvāja’s seed was spilled upon seeing Urvaśī.
He deposited his seed in a wooden vessel (droṇa);
therefore, that preceptor became known as Droṇa.
From him, Kṛpī indeed obtained Aśvatthāman, who was a portion of Śaṅkara.
In former times, Kaca was the son born to Bṛhaspati from his two wives;
during the Vaivasvata Manvantara, he became a treasury of asceticism and a disciple of Śukra.
"May that science not exist for him," he commanded;
"let there be no lord of the earth afflicted by passion"—
thus the sage uttered a curse.
Having obtained the Mṛtasañjīvinī [mantra] from him, he then went somewhere;
in the forest, he desired to practice its yoga with Devayānī, the daughter of his guru.
"He should study together with his disciples; let the non-twice-born be the master"—thus says Ātman, for even among the disciples mentioned by the poet, [the former] would be superior. (PS 2.6.52)
The daughter of King Devayaśas, who had been taught the Vedas by Śakradharṣaṇa, cast the semen of her teacher into the water while she was playing in the water with her friends. (PS 2.6.53)
Because her own garment was taken away, she became distressed by the insult to herself,
like the princess Devayānī when her clothes were snatched away in the lake.
When the princess had departed, Yayāti, born of the lunar dynasty, arrived before her and was then wandering for the sake of hunting.
Having lifted her up while she was naked, the king gave her his own upper garment;
having taken it, she reached her home, and then the king returned to his own city.
For that purpose, having learned that Śukra was angry, the king propitiated him and offered his own daughter as a maidservant to the preceptor’s daughter.
Śukra joyfully gave his own daughter to King Yayāti, accompanied by Śarmiṣṭhā as a maidservant; for it was right that the virtuous woman should become a servant to the king.
Yadu’s son was born of Devayānī; from him arose that lineage born of Kṛtavīrya, namely Arjuna, who, having subdued the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, recovered it once again.
Although he clearly possessed a pair of thousands of arms,
Hari was born from Vasudeva, who was the son of an Apsaras born in that lineage and had been given away after being carried off.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second section of the Śrī Prakāśasaṃhitā.
